(e)                Marketing of coir and coir products in India and abroad.
(f)                 Preventing unfair competition among producers and exporters.
(g)                Assisting in the setting up of units for the manufacture of products.
(h)                Promoting cooperative organizations among producers of husks, coir fibre, coir yarn and manufacturers
of coir products.
(i)                  Ensuring remunerative returns to producers and manufacturers.
 
5.1       India is the world’s largest producer of coir. The coir industry is labour intensive and provide employment to
more than five lakh persons of which women constitute 80 per cent. The production of coir and coir products has been
rising continuously. The production of coir fibre has risen from 2,96,000 metric tones in 1997-98 to 3,64,000 metric
tones in 1999-2000. The export of coir and coir products has also been increasing from Rs.238.93 crores in the year
1997-98 to Rs.313 crores in 2000-01. Though India is the largest producer of coir, its contribution in world trade is
small due to low technology. Only 30% of the coconut husk is utilized for coir production. Coir Board is taking a
number of steps to improve productivity, export potential and better utilization of the raw material. These are :-
·
  Significant Research and Development activities in areas like Coir Geotextiles for soil and water conservation
and Coirret for speeding up the retting process.
·  Blended fibres are used for more value added products and a wider product range. MoU signed with NID,
Ahmedabad for collaborative research on design and product development  which includes blending of coir with
other natural fibres like sisal, jute, palmirah, banana, pineapple etc.
·  Coir Board is providing increasing support for brown fibre activities. White fibre is restricted to Kerala only
while brown fibre is available in all the other coir producing states.
·  Coir board is promoting increased   mechanization for higher productivity.
·  UNDP project for technology   transfer, modernization and capacity building at a cost of US $ 846,000.
·  Export promotion    activities   like participation  in fairs and festivals are taken up by the Coir Board.
5.2       A new Market Development Assistance (MDA) scheme has been introduced in Coir Sector. This scheme has
replaced the existing "Rebate Scheme" and provides financial assistance @ 10 per cent to the Apex Cooperative

74th Report of Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/74threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:15:39]
Societies, Primary Co-operative Societies, Public Sector Enterprises in the coir industry,  Showrooms/Sales Depot of
Coir Board on the basis of gross annual sales turnover.
5.3       Coir Industry was traditionally confined to Kerala due to the abundant availability of raw-material and natural
facilities for retting. It is a labour intensive, export oriented cottage industry employing 5.43  lakh people. The rapid
expansion of coconut cultivation in the non-traditional areas increased the availability of raw-material and consequently
the coir industry spread to non-traditional areas like Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh and  Orissa and  West
Bengal.
5.4       In view of the growing competition in coir and coir products from the countries like Sri Lanka, China, Vietnam
etc. the coir yarn products have been removed from the purview of Minimum Export Price  (MEP)  from 17
th July, 
2001. This is the first step towards deregulation.
5.5       The five year EXIM policy announced on 1 st April, 2002 seeks to enable  Indian artisans, Cottage and Small
Industries to venture out overseas and adopt the world  as their market. The new  policy makes exports free, easy and
possibly rewarding. This  assumes special significance especially when India ranks low in global competition given
global slowdown and domestic recession. The Exim policy is comprehensive,  encompassing agro sector, cottage and
handicrafts and small scale sectors thus taking care of more than 80% the population living in rural areas.
5.6       The Committee, therefore, recommends that in view of the importance of this sector, diversified forms  of coir
products  and product-mix   should be attempted.  Research programmes should be undertaken by the Coir Board for
improving the quality of the coir fibre, for enhancing the export of coir products such as the green husk fibre produced
in the non-traditional coir producing areas using “coirret”. The Committee also notes that the market for  coir pith, a
waste material of the coir industry converted into one of the major export items in the list of coir products, remains 
untapped and the potential for the export of coir pith is excellent. The Committee, therefore, recommends that all out
efforts should be made to make  pith export achieve its fullest potential.
5.7       Nearly 80% of the coir workers in the fibre extraction and spinning sector are women. The production and
processing methods in coir  industry continue to be traditional. The coir industry has the potential to provide
employment at low investment cost and a large number of people from the socially and  economically weaker sections
of the society depend on this industry. It is for this reason that the establishment of coir industry in India gains added
significance.
5.8       During the BE 2002-03 Coir Industries have been allocated an amount of Rs.16.20 crores as plan and Rs.2.76
crores as non-plan (total 18.96 crore) against a plan provision of Rs.18 crores and non-plan provision of Rs.5.11 crores
in  BE 2001-02 and 11.60 crores as plan and Rs.2.62 crores as a non-plan in the RE for 2001-02.
5.9       The Committee observes that Coir Sector employs   5 lakh people and it has the potential of expanding its
activities. Although the fund allocation for the sector has been doubled in the 9
th five year plan from what it was in the
8th five year plan, (Rs.31 crores during the 8 th five year Plan and Rs.60 crores during the 9 th five year Plan), this sector
is still under-budgeted. There is further scope for absorbing funds in this sector particularly in the non-traditional areas
such as Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh, Orissa, West Bengal, Andaman and Nicobar Islands where new
products could be developed.  The Committee therefore recommends that the allocation for the Coir Industry should be
revised so that attention can be focused on providing more employment opportunities in this sector.   
5.10     For the first time in the history of coir industry, a Group Personal Accident Insurance Scheme has been
introduced in coir sector. Under this scheme a coir worker who meets with accidental death, permanent total disability
or partial total disability is eligible for compensation upto Rs. 25,000.
5.11     The Committee appreciates the measure for welfare of the people, especially women, engaged in the coir
industry which  remains unorganised to a great extent. The Committee hopes that more such initiatives  would be  taken
in near future  for the benefit of large number of people engaged in the industry.

TINY AND MICRO ENTERPRISES
9          Tiny enterprises are an important component of the SSI sector whose relative share in village and small
industries is increasing. The sector is important since it utilizes local raw material, provides employment to local
manpower and caters broadly to local market. This sector however, suffers from weak financial structure, use of
traditional and obsolete technology resulting into poor quality goods and having no access to the economies of scale.
These are basically one man shows and lack modern and efficient entrepreneurship.
9.1       The tiny sector enjoys distinct advantage of its ability to utilize local resource and skill. They cater to local needs
and generate substantial employment opportunities. However, they suffer from certain inherent weaknesses :-
(i)
                  Very poor capital base and difficulty in raising institutional credit
(ii)                Lack of infrastructure facilities particularly power
(iii)               Inadequate access to appropriate technology
(iv)              Problems in marketing the produce on account of quality, cost and inability to adopt    the required
marketing techniques
(v)                Inadequate competitive abilities
(vi)              Inability to cope up with plethora of laws, rules and regulations
(vii)      Lack of entrepreneurial skills and training
9.2       The Committee observes that tiny and micro enterprises are  the most  vulnerable sector in the era of free
imports and intense  competition.  The sector is most threatened  in the face of challenges thrown from China and cheap
imports from Nepal. Office of Development Commissioner (Small Scale Industries) should see that concern of tiny
sector are addressed  adequately and optimum assistance may be provided to them to tide over hurdles faced by them
like poor capital base, lack of infrastructure, obsolete technology marketing and competitiveness etc.  In view of the
importance of this sector, appropriate measures for promotion of tiny sector by the Govt. may be taken by reorienting its
policies.

should be fixed and better budget management  undertaken. This would be a major step forward.   The Committee
recommends further that expenditure frame-work needs to be strengthened. This would involve identifying current and
future financial requirements, and deviations from the prescribed procedure should not be allowed under any
circumstances.  
(Para 3.28)
 
            The   Committee finds that non-plan allocation for Khadi and Village Industries  shows an increasing trend. It is
also not managed efficiently  while KVIC is  over-staffed. The  Committee recommends that KVIC should undertake
trimming exercise for reducing surplus staff by extending VRS in order to curtail non-plan expenditure and to make the
institution economically viable.
(Para 3.30)
 
            The Committee observes that the report of Arthur Andersen was submitted in September, 2000 and  is still under
examination by the KVIC. The Committee recommends that the examination of the report be expedited and a final view
be taken without further delay.
(Para 3.32)
 
            The Committee expresses serious concern that the stocks of goods worth several hundred crores are lying locked
and unused.  Perhaps this is why, KVIC  has been experiencing working capital difficulties. If this state of affairs 
continues, KVIC  will not only be faced with resource crunch as the money remains locked up and stocks lying unsold
but also lose customer base as there will be no takers for the old stocks.
(Para 3.35)
 
The Committee therefore  recommends that KVIC should dispose of the old stock as early as possible even by 
providing heavy discounts and recover money. KVIC may utilize the revenue earned on fresh inventory and recycle the
money. KVIC should keep fresh inventory as  old inventory  would not fetch much money.
(Para 3.36)

            The Committee observes that poor quality and poor designs have resulted in poor sales and accumulation of 
large inventories.The working cycle of production sales-cash-realization for Khadi is long and substantial funds are
blocked as working capital  for Khadi institutions. This has adversely affected performance.
(Para 3.37)
            The Committee, therefore, recommends that  CCPC  should henceforth undertake  periodical review of the stock
build up before approving the quantities to be purchased. Further, responsibility for the lapses for allocating of funds
and  excess  stocking of cotton on the part of officials/non-officials should be fixed.
(Para 3.41)
 
            The Committee recommends that the following policy support measures should be extended to Khadi and
Village Industries to give it  further boost :-
 
(i)               Most of the states have given sales tax exemption to KVI products,  however, Value added-tax is to
come into force w.e.f. 1.4.2003.  KVI Sector should be exempted from value added tax, octroi, entry tax etc.
 
(ii)     Existing labour laws, by and large exit to safeguard the interest of organized labour in large and medium
industries. High Power Committee headed by the thenPrime Minister Shri Narasimha Rao recommended
exemption of KVI sector from the existing labour laws as artisans are mostly self-employed. A policy decision 
in the matter should be taken at the earliest.
 
(iii)    Financial institutions have started playing important role from mid 1990s after introduction of REGP. But still
now the investment is very low compared to other areas in priority sector. Special earmarking for KVI sector is
felt necessary.
 
(iv)
      Preferential purchase support as is available to certain sectors is not there for KVI sector. The policy decision
for state and central governments to purchase a minimum percentage of utility articles from KVI sector will
give boost to the sector.
 
(v)
        Declaration of KVIC as Export Promotion Council for KVI products will promote export of KVI goods and
create potential for exports.
(Para 3.42)
           
The Committee observes that  in spite of KVIC’s repeated request over the years, funds flow to KVI Institutions
from Banks under ISEC is not upto the desired level. Analysis of ISECs  issued by KVIC  and actual funds made
available by Banks against the ISEC indicates that in the recent past the gap in the ISEC value vis-à-vis fund provided
by Banks goes to be extent of  50%.
(Para 4.2)
            The Committee, therefore, recommends that the Govt. of India/RBI may take appropriate policy decision so that
Banks are  bound to honour the ISECs issued by the KVIC to its full extent.
(Para 4.3)

            While addressing the concerns of KVI sector, the impact of globalisation, availability of latest technology,
multiplicity   and inadequate infrastructure have to be taken into account. At the same time, in order to meet the
challenges of   global competition, the Village Industries products have to be competitive in terms of quality, packaging,
pricing etc.  The Committee therefore recommends that continuous efforts need to be made for  improving the quality,
design and marketing of Village Industries products.  In order to achieve these objectives,   existing R&D facilities need
to be enhanced to facilitate Village Industries to introduce innovation, quality assurance and standardization. Last but
not least, a holistic approach is required  to be made to achieve the goal of  improving the functioning of KVIC.
(Para 4.4)
 
            The five year EXIM policy announced on 1
st April, 2002 seeks to enable  Indian artisans, Cottage and Small
Industries to venture out overseas and adopt the world  as their market. The new  policy makes exports free, easy and
possibly rewarding. This  assumes special significance especially when India ranks low in global competition given
global slowdown and domestic recession. The Exim policy is comprehensive,  encompassing agro sector, cottage and
handicrafts and small scale sectors thus taking care of more than 80% the population living in rural areas.
(Para 5.5)
 
            The Committee, therefore, recommends that in view of the importance of this sector, diversified forms  of coir
products  and product-mix   should be attempted.  Research programmes should be undertaken by the Coir Board for
improving the quality of the coir fibre, for enhancing the export of coir products such as the green husk fibre produced
in the non-traditional coir producing areas using “coirret”. The Committee also notes that the market for  coir pith, a
waste material of the coir industry converted into one of the major export items in the list of coir products, remains

efforts should be made to make  pith export achieve its fullest potential.

activities. Although the fund allocation for the sector has been doubled in the 9
th five year plan from what it was in the
8th five year plan, (Rs.31 crores during the 8 th five year Plan and Rs.60 crores during the 9 th five year Plan), this sector
is still under-budgeted. There is further scope for absorbing funds in this sector particularly in the non-traditional areas
such as Tamil Nadu, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh, Orissa, West Bengal, Andaman and Nicobar Islands where new
products could be developed.  The Committee therefore recommends that the allocation for the Coir Industry should be
revised so that attention can be focused on providing more employment opportunities in this sector.   
(Para 5.9)
            The Committee appreciates the measure for welfare of the people, especially women, engaged in the coir
industry which  remains unorganised to a great extent. The Committee hopes that more such initiatives  would be  taken
in near future  for the benefit of large number of people engaged in the industry.
(Para 5.11)
 
            The Committee observes that only a third of the target  could be achieved in the case of PMRY during the year
2001-02 (upto December, 2001) It is inconceivable how the two third of the target could be achieved during the
remaining three months of the year. The Committee, therefore, recommends that setting of the targets should go along

wise within a stipulated time frame.

as shown above.  The Committee had hoped that with the creation of  new Ministry, the target and allocation for the
scheme would be increased,  but the Committee finds that the target set during the last four years of PMRY has remain
unchanged i.e   2.20 lakhs  The Committee therefore, recommends that taking into consideration the importance of the

allocation may be enhanced for the purpose.
(Para 6.7)
 
            The Committee observes that the crux of the problem lies in the recovery scenario under PMRY which has been
showing a  decreasing trend   If this sort of thing continues,  there will be less  funds available year by year  to
channelise for future schemes as the money will be in short supply. A stage  may come  that the  scheme may have to be
closed down due to non-availability of funds. The Committee, therefore, recommends   that recovery of loans,  which is
a grey area in the present scenario, should be given more attention and loopholes in this regard should be plugged  so
that the scheme may not be scuttled for want of funds in future  and recycling of funds may continue. The
Chairman/Managing Directors – All India Scheduled Commercial Banks may be suitably advised by the RBI to
improve their recovery performance to recycle the funds and constitute `recovery cells’ at Regional/ Zonal  office level.
(Para 6.9)
 
            The Committee further observes that though the Government achieved in some measure quantitative target of the
PMRY,  no efforts were made either by the Govt. or by other agencies to evaluate the qualitative achievement of the
scheme. The beneficiaries experienced difficulties in starting and running the venture. The major problem in starting the
unit was in getting the loan. 50% of the beneficiaries were affected by the delay in disbursement of the loan. This forced
them to take loan from  moneylenders  at a very high rate of interest and this had an adverse effect on their business.
The beneficiaries reported that because of the financial delay they could not reach  their  expectations. The beneficiaries
of the category made default in payment of loan.
(Para 6.10)
 
            The Committee finds that shortage of funds for working capital is hindering the PMRY beneficiaries. They could
not execute  their  orders in time due to shortage of funds and for marketing capital requirements, they resort to private
money lenders at a high rate of interest resulting in the increased cost of production and short fall in profit margin.
(Para 6.11)
 
            The high cost of operation is another problem where 20% of the industries were affected by this and  they could 
not compete in the local market. Increase in the cost of spare parts are the main cost accelerating items and
entrepreneurs could not  repay- the interest in time. The entrepreneurs could not adjust  themselves  to the demand and
supply mechanism of the market.
(Para 6.12)
 
            As regards the undue delay in giving loans by banks, the Committee impresses upon banks to avoid undue
delay.  The Committee recommends that implementing banks should be advised by the RBI to sanction the applications
within the prescribed time frame and speedily dispose off the same to ensure that there is no inordinate gap between the
sanction and disbursement of loan. DICs should play a pro-active role in this regard. RBI`s guidelines for disposing of
applications under PMRY within the time period of thirty days must be adhered to by banks.
(Para 6.13)
 
            As  regards the delay in getting power connection, the Committee desires that Government should take suitable

order to implement the REGP/Margin Money Scheme, KVIC has also placed Margin Money  Grant with State/UT KVI

 REPORT
 
1.1       The Ministry of Small Scale Industries is the nodal ministry for policy formulation, promotion, development and
protection of small scale industries. It also monitors the implementation of these policies.
1.2       Ministry of SSI designs and implements the policies through its field organizations for promotion and growth of
small enterprises. The Ministry also coordinates with other Ministries/Departments on behalf of the Small Scale
Industries (SSI) sector.
1.3       Implementation of   policies and various programmes/schemes for providing infrastructure and support services
to small enterprises is undertaken through its attached office, namely the Small Industries Development Organisation
(SIDO).
1.4              Small Scale Sector is an integral part of the Indian economy. It has contributed significantly in the overall
economic development of the country and has provided vibrancy to its economy. Today, there are 3.2   million
registered small units in the country employing 18 million persons. In terms of value addition, it contributes 40 per cent
of the manufacturing sector production and its share in the total exports of the country is around 36 per cent. This sector
is the largest employment generator next to agriculture.
1.5              The overall performance of this sector during the last few years has been better than the performance of the
industrial sector as a whole. This sector has the potential to withstand change. It produces more than 8,000 items
varying from the simple to the most sophisticated products, using state-of-the-art technology. However, with
liberalization and opening up of the Indian economy, this sector is now facing tremendous challenges, albeit with
sufficient opportunities for growth.
1.6       The process of liberalization and market reforms has created wide-ranging opportunities for the development of
small-scale industries. At the same time, changing world scenario has thrown up new challenges to the very existence of
the sector. Moreover, this sector has also been facing some problems related to credit, infrastructure, technology,
marketing, delayed payments, problems on account of complex rules and regulation etc.  The need of the hour is to
suitably strengthen the sector so that it can adapt itself to the changed environment and face challenges boldly and
effectively. In order to enable this sector to avail the opportunities and play its role as an engine of growth, the Hon’ble
Prime Minister on 30
th August 2000 announced a Comprehensive Policy Package for the SSI Sector.
1.7       The small enterprise has emerged as a focus area for forging and promoting trade. Economic reform programmes
envisage the emergence of Indian Industry as a global competitor with substantial presence in the international markets.
Technology upgradation and modernization of SSI sector and promotion of export from this sector are interlinked
issues, which are important objectives behind promoting international cooperation. Nine countries viz; USA, Germany,
Italy, South Korea, U.K., Taiwan, Japan, Singapore and Israel have been identified as the thrust countries for promoting
enterprise-to-enterprise cooperation to upgrade the capabilities of Indian SSI sector to make it competitive in the global

markets. This has assumed greater significance in the context of the liberalization process. In fact, the potential of SSI
sector for contributing to exports and creating employment remains untapped in the absence of access to technology and

VI.      CREDIT TO SSI SECTOR
6.1       One of the major problems of SSls is that of finance, whether it is equity, term loan or working capital. Financial
institutions and commercial banks are often reluctant to lend to small scale enterprises because of the high risks
involved. Moreover, the commercial banks and financial institutions that provide working capital and term finance to
the corporate borrower generally demand personal guarantees from borrowers, besides collateral. This adversely affects
the borrowing capacity of the small entrepreneur. The lack of coordination between commercial banks and financial
institutions causes delay in availability of working capital and hence in the commissioning of projects. The complex and
time-consuming procedures and formalities of the institutional lenders cause operational impediments for SSI units.
6.2       The Ministry has apprised the Committee that the net bank credit outstanding to SSI sector has increased from
Rs. 45, 789 crores as on 31.3.2000 to Rs. 48, 445 crores on 31.3.2001.  In order to further increase the flow of credit, the

(with reasons) of loan applications. However, they need to follow it sincerely. Further, once a loan has been sanctioned,
a time frame for the release of various installments should be committed in accordance with the needs of the
entrepreneurs. It must also be ensured that with the provision of the concept of single window, the time involved in
making the disbursements is considerably reduced. As far as the National Equity Fund (NEF) scheme is concerned, it

substantial advantage from it.

7.1       The Government introduced the Credit Guarantee Fund Scheme for Small Industries in May 2000 with the
objective of making credit available to SSI units, particularly tiny units, for loans up to Rs.10 lakh without
collateral/third party guarantees. The Scheme is being operated by the Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Small Industries
(CGTSI) set up jointly by the Government of India and SIDBI. The loan limit underthe Scheme, which was Rs.10 lakh
per borrower, has been enhanced to Rs.25 lakh per borrower in terms of the Comprehensive Policy Package on SSI
announced by the Hon’ble Prime Minister on 30
th August, 2000, when the Scheme was formally launched.
7.2       The Scheme covers collateral free credit facility (term loan and/or working capital) extended by eligible lending
institutions to new and existing SSI Units including Information Technology and Software Industry, up to Rs.25 lakh
per borrowing unit. The Guarantee cover would be up to 75% of the credit subject to maximum guarantee limit of
Rs.18.75 lakh. The lending institutions availing guarantee from theTrust have to pay a one time guarantee fee of 2.5% of
the Credit facility (comprising term loan and/or working capital) sanctioned by the lending institution to the borrower
and annual service fee of 1% per annum on the outstanding loan amount on 31
st March of each year.
7.3       The Credit Guarantee Scheme was initially approved for one year with a corpus of Rs.125 crore contributed by
the Government of India and SIDBI in the ratio of 4:1. Subsequently, the Government decided to continue the Scheme

Industries to guarantee loans up to Rs.25 lakh.  The Corpus fund of CGTSI was enhanced to Rs.200 crore with a further

8.1       The Committee observes that in order to encourage new entrepreneurs to set up small scale units, it is very

scale units in Software / Information Technology sector, SIDBI has taken an initiative in the launching of the State /

easily available to very small and tiny units. EXIM Bank has also made an entry into venture capital finance by

8.2       The Committee recommends that more venture funds in high-growth sectors such as information technology,

which a new concept company, the venture business, could take root during a short period of time. As a result, the

XI.       ANTI DUMPING MEASURES
11.1     There is expected to be large scale dumping of different products and flow of cheaper imports to Indian markets.
Imported consumer goods being of international standards in quality and competitive in prices are likely to change the
tastes of Indian consumers. It may prove to be a major factor in shrinking demand for local products. SSls are struggling
to restructure themselves, diversify production, adopt higher standards, and have collaborations for product designs or
brands or upgraded technology for their existence. There is ignorance among small scale entrepreneurs about
implications of WTO provisions in general and removal of QRs in particular. SSls did not get much time to adjust and
prepare themselves for increased competition and are thus in a precarious situation.
11.2     The Committee recommends that on account of almost all products coming under Open General License (OGL)
list, the Government may further strengthen the anti-dumping mechanism so that remedial measures may be initiated
expeditiously.  Countervailing duties and safeguard duties may be imposed in order to protect domestic producers from
cheap imports.  It may not be possible for SSIs units to function   in such a competitive market.  However, if they want
to grow from SSI level, all facilities available to them should continue for at least five years.
11.3.  The Representative of Laghu Udyog Bharati stated
“In the treaty with Nepal, I understand, we have put a clause that only those goods which are having some
manufacturing content   of Nepalese origin are exempt from our import duty. Actually what is happening is, so many
sham units are now being established there in Nepal and the goods are coming from Nepal and hurting the small-scale

11.5     The Committee, therefore, recommends that Government should closely monitor the dumping of goods from

11.6     The Committee observes that the major option for limiting imports that remains for use by policy-makers in a
QR-free regime is that of higher tariffs. The Committee recommends that QRs may be converted into tariff and non-
tariff equivalents to give an adequate protection to the domestic SSls. While this measure would be a discouraging
factor for foreign producers to export their cheap goods to India, it would also mean increasing revenue for the
Government of India.
11.7     The Committee, therefore, recommends tariff and non-tariff barriers may be imposed in the form of higher
safety standards, and sanitary and phyto-sanitary measures as are permissible within the WTO framework.
11.8     The Committee further recommends that compulsory printing of manufacturing date, maximum retail price (in
Indian rupees) and composition of the products, by foreign exporters should be introduced. This would, of course, be
compatible with the national obligation under WTO, as domestic manufacturers are already required to comply with
these requirements.
XII.       SICKNESS IN SSI SECTOR
12.1     The small scale industry in India faces a number of problems leading to growing industrial sickness. According
to the RBI Report on Trend and Progress of Banking in India, there were 3,06,013 sick / weak 551 units in 1999. An
amount of Rs 4,313 crore of outstanding bank credit was locked up in these units. Out of the total sick / weak units,
18,692 units have been identified as potentially viable. Amongst these, 12, 759 have been put under nursing programme
by banks.
12.2     The Ministry has informed that Sickness in SSI Sector is a matter of constant concern. A number of measures
have been taken from time to time to reduce the incidence of sickness in the small scale sector. The incidence of
sickness in the sector has come down consistently from 306,221 sick SSI units as on March 1999 to 2,49,360 sick SSI
units as on March 2001.
  12.3      To tackle the problem of rehabilitation of potentially viable sick SSI units, the RBI constituted a Working
Group on 25th November 2000 under the chairmanship of Shri S.S.Kohli, the then Chairman of Indian Banks
Association, to look into the issue. The Working Group submitted its Report in May 2001. All the major
recommendations of the Working Group have been accepted by the RBI, including a change in the definition of sick SSI
units, norms for deciding on the viability of sick units, etc. The revised definition would enable Banks to take action at
an early stage for revival of the units. Based on the accepted recommendations of the Working Group, the RBI has
drawn up the Revised Guidelines for Rehabilitation of Sick SSI Units, which have been circulated on 16th January 2002
to all the Banks for implementation.
12.4        The Committee recommends that all banks should take effective steps to help sick SSIs restructure
themselves.  The Committee observes that the abolition of Sick Industries Companies Act (SICA) so as to facilitate
prompt winding up of unviable enterprise and swift redeployment of their resources in production remains a promise.
Similarly, on the Competition Law, nothing has been done. It has reached only the stage of Parliamentary consideration.
It has not become a law. 
12.5         The Committee recommends that action may be taken in regard to Abolition of Sick Industries Companies
Act.  Further, Ministry should endeavour to see that Competition Law is enacted soon.
In order to revive sick industries, the Committee recommends further: -
(a)                A special fund may be created for rehabilitation of sick SSls and the commercial banks may earmark a

portion of loans to ailing SSls.
(b)               The State Level Inter Institutional Committees (SLIICs) need to be revitalised and DICs may be used as
a forum to redress the grievances regarding delays in rehabilitation.
(c)                An Arbitration Clause may also be included in all borrower-lender arrangements in terms of Indian
Arbitration Act to avoid protracted litigation and costs. Although Entrepreneurship Development through
small enterprises is basically owner-managed, a significant number of them do employ persons for
performing managerial functions. The SSI units on the growth path should encourage their key personnel
to think and work more as entrepreneurs than as mere employees.
XIII.      EXCISE DUTY EXEMPTION
13.1    Excise exemption makes SSI products cost effective and strengthens their competitiveness. Excise exemption
was enhanced from Rs.50 Lakhs to Rs.l crore in September 2001.
13.2     It has been observed that in respect of certain products, the duties of excise and custom on raw
materials/intermediate goods are higher than on the finished goods. This is anomalous as it makes the SSI units difficult
to avail MODVAT (now CENVAT) in case of excise duty and discourages value addition in the country in case of
custom duty.
13.3     In view of the above, the Committee feels that there is need for ensuring harmonisation of tax structure by
providing the following:-
(a)
    Rationalisation of duty may be ensured on finished goods vis-a-vis their raw           materials or intermediate
goods.
(b)   Capital Gains Exemptionmay be given to sick SSI units selling off their fixed assets to repay bank loans.
(c)    The coverage of Excise Duty Exemption Scheme may be made available to all the items produced by the small
scale units.
(d)   Under MRP based assessment an additional 10% rebate may be allowed to SSI units. Rationalisation of
customs duty on raw materials/intermediate goods and finished goods for Uninterrupted Power Supplies (UPS),
components/parts of domestic electrical appliances, components/parts of auto bulbs, umbrella components,
plastic raw materials, lead ingots, electric copper wires, parts and components of RF and IF coils and reduction
of custom duty on low carbon Ferro chrome and linear alkyl benzene (LAB) may also be done.      
XIV.    MARKETING & EXPORTS
14.1     Marketing, for both domestic and export markets, has all along been a major problem area for the small scale
industry. Though the Price and Purchase Preference Policy has been in existence for a long time, there is need to take
several other measures.
14.2
          Finance is a major area, which small scale units report as a major impediment for marketing. The credit
extended by the units to their customers, to the trade and to the Government departments, and public sector enterprises,
blocks a major part of their funds.
14.3
          The Committee recommends that banks and other financial institutions provide marketing oriented financial
assistance to small scale sector, particularly for advertising, product promotion and setting up of regional marketing
offices. Factoring services by the banks may also be given greater priority.
14.4   Market Development Assistance (MDA) Programme has been launched for SSI Associations for participating in
international fairs, exhibitions, collection of information on marketing/exports, conducting surveys for filing anti-

may be done.

XV.      TECHNOLOGY UPGRADATION
15.1     The technological upgradation of the SSI units in India has been quite slow. There are a number of factors that
are responsible for this. The Indian market has so far been basically a sellers' market. Therefore, entrepreneurs have not
made any efforts for modernisation. Moreover, there is non-availability of proper information regarding latest
technologies and their suppliers. There is inadequate availability of credit for investment in technological upgradation
and testing facilities are also not readily available. Even the technological institutions set up for assisting the small scale
industries themselves lack sophistication and coordination amongst each other.
(a) For effective technological upgradation in Indian SSI units, the Committee recommends that the partnership
approach to develop linkages between large and small enterprises be strengthened.
(b) Technology Bureau for International Industrial Partnerships and Technology Bureau for Small Enterprises,
Delhi has been providing useful services for technology upgradation in the small scale units. These organisations
need to be strengthened further and their activities need to be marketed / advertised in an effective manner. The
small scale industries in India have added strength to the industrial infrastructure and have been the engine of
growth for industrialisation. However, they are known for producing poor quality products. This makes the Indian
goods less competitive in the international markets.
(C)  The Committee observes that Government has set up a number of organizations for the purpose of
technological upgradation and quality improvement in the SS1 units. However, most of these facilities are either
non-functional or grossly under-utilised. There is an urgent need to revamp the whole system and make it effective
and beneficial to the small industries.
(d)               The Committee further recommends that quality training to significantly improve quality by creating
awareness among personnel about meeting customer requirements, standardizing processes, training operatives and
enforcing technical discipline should be institutionalized. There is a need to conduct a comprehensive research
study in a sample of SSI units to determine areas of waste and non-value adding activities and develop
methodology for quality improvement and cost reduction programmes. Further 1SO 9000 certification. may be
made more attractive to introduce quality-consciousness among small entrepreneurs. BIS standards may also be
upgraded from time to time in tune with the developments in quality worldwide.
 
XVI.    LABOUR REFORMS IN SSIs
16.1     The Committee observes that the present structure of labour laws does not encourage efficient performance by
the SSls. Managements find it difficult to manage their human resources optimally because of the constrained labour
laws. As of now, the same set of labour laws is applicable to all industrial undertakings, irrespective of their size.
16.2     The Committee therefore, recommends that instead of a plethora of labour laws, a single unified Act with simple
provisions understandable by the entrepreneurs of SSI units be legislated. SSI units employing upto 50 persons should
be kept outside the purview of the labour law. Instead of the complex Industrial Disputes Act, a simpler law to govern
the relationship between the Employer and the Employee be made applicable. The Shops and Establishments may also
be suitably modified.
16.3     The Committee further observes that the existing social security legislations such as Employees' Provident Fund

& Miscellaneous Provisions Act, Employees State Insurance act, Maternity Benefits Act, Workmen's Compensation
Act, and the Payment of Gratuity Act are very cumbersome for entrepreneurs of small scale units to understand and
comply with. The Committee therefore recommends that instead of so many social security legislations, a
comprehensive Social Security Scheme be formulated for providing for one insurance cover to each workman. The

XVII.  MULTIPLICITY OF AGENCIES
17.1     The Committee observes that at present, there are several Government agencies to deal with small scale
industries in India. These include Ministry of SSI & ARI, Office of Development Commissioner (SSI), Small Industries
Development Organisation, Small Industries Service Institutes, National Small Industries Corporation, Small Industries
development Bank of India, Product-cum-process Development Centres, Regional Testing Centres, District Industries
Centres, State Financial Corporations, State Industrial Development Corporations, State Small Industries Development
Corporations, etc.
17.2     The Committee, therefore, recommends that roles of all these organisations be re-evaluated and clearly defined.
It needs to be ensured that their activities do not overlap each other. There should also be co-ordination in the activities
of these agencies. Most importantly, all of these should be able to provide effective service to the small scale sector.
 
XVIII. DE-RESERVATION OF SSI ITEMS
18.1     As required by WTO, India   removed all quantitative restrictions (QRs) by 31st March 2001.The Union Minister
for Commerce announced the removal of restrictions while announcing the EXIM policy for 2002-07. While the impact
of the removal of QRs is being felt directly by industries, which were earlier protected, there is likely to be greater
impact on the SSls, especially with regard to their competitive ability and integration with the global markets against the
opportunities of an expanding global market.
18.2     The policy of reservation, was not brought as a measure of protection alone, but was brought for some other
factors as well such as provisions of employment opportunities, development of industrial activities in the backward and
rural areas, utilization of local raw-materials, restraining migration of labour etc. Large industries and MNCs are not
barred from manufacturing the reserved items.  They have only to adhere to the stipulation that 50% of their production
of the reserved items should be exported, which they could easily do with their latest technologies and their professional
management. 
18.3    De-reservation of over 50 items which were marked for exclusive production in the SSI sector has hit hard such
affected and related units.  The Committee   fails to see any supportive and promotional measure in the latest Budget for
such affected units.  It is to be noted that the Government had accepted the Abid Hussain Committee Report in full in
1997.  The Abid Hussain Committee recommended that the abolition of reservation should accompany a support
package for the small industries, which include equity support, interest rate concessions, technology assistance etc.  The
Abid Hussain Committee, therefore, recommended allocation of Rs. 500 crore per year i.e. Rs.2, 500 crore over the next
five years for the purpose.
18.4     The Committee feels that the Government should have given such a package to the affected units. This may
include timely and low cost credit; export assistance and proper infrastructure facilities. After giving the package, a time
frame may be simultaneously given to such affected units to enable them to fight for survival.  In the absence of such
package, the Committee feels the units might be hard-pressed to survive.  Moreover, effecting dereservation without any
package will bring deleterious socio economic changes as reservation directly affects employment and economic
growth.

19.1     Small Industries Development Organisation (SIDO), Ministry of Small Scale Industries, Government of India
has been operating a number of promotional schemes for the growth of the small scale industries in the country.  The
Integrated Infrastructural Development Scheme is one such Scheme to facilitate the location of industries in rural
backward areas and to generate employment opportunities by establishing close linkages between agriculture and

Centre Rs. 5.00 crore in the ratio of 2:3 and the cost in excess thereof is met by State/UT Governments.  Suitable land

XX.      DELAYED PAYMENT TO SSIs
20.1     The Committee observes that the Delayed Payment to SSIs by large company continues to be a major problem
for SSIs sector.   SSI Association informed the Committee that there is a delayed payment Act to sort out the problems
but that has failed to give the desired results. SSI associations have also been suggesting that some punitive action be
taken against those large companies, which make undue delay in making payment to the small scale sector. Whenever
they file their income tax returns, certain amount should be charged from them. If there is some outstanding bill and
they have not paid them on account of delay payment, that amount should be adjusted at the time of filing the returns.
20.2    The Secretary, Ministry of Small Scale Industries   stated during his oral evidence before the Committee on 2
nd
April, 2002, “there have been delayed payment incidence all over the country to the small scale sector which affect the
finance availability.  We suggest that a delayed payment Act should be there by Parliament   and it should be made more
stringent so that the payments are received in due time”
20.3    The Committee, therefore, recommends that stringent action should be taken against the erring large companies
which have failed to make payment to SSIs in due time.   Necessary amendment for taking punitive   action may also
be   contemplated in the Delayed Payment Act.
 
XXI.      NON-PERFORMING ASSETS (NPA)       
21.1     The Committee has been apprised that banks have to follow the guidelines issued recently   in respect of NPA by
the Reserve Bank of India.  It has been made mandatory for banks to convert the loans, if whole installment remains
unpaid, into NPAs within three to six months; otherwise they have to face harsh action.  Due to these guidelines banks
will always be very conservative in extending loans to SSIs.  Because of   such guidelines issued by RBI, SSIs will
suffer and face difficulty   in getting   the loan advances.
21.2     The Committee therefore, recommends that RBI should review the guidelines issued in respect of NPA to
banks   and should prescribe that no loan asset would become NPA even if the loan installments or interest remains
overdue   for a period of one year
 
XXII.   PURCHASE PREFERENCE FOR SSI SECTOR
22.1     In   USA, there are special laws for small scale sector.  But in our country, there is no such provision for small
scale sector.  Moreover, 50 items have been de-reserved which were exclusively reserved for the Small Scale Sector. 
Marketing facilities for the Small Scale Sector are also not adequate.   Majority of the consumption of items
manufactured by Small Scale Sector is for domestic consumption.  Only 8-10% of the items made by SSIs is exported.
22.2     The Committee therefore, recommends that in order to protect small scale sector from multinational companies
and others, a certain % of items, say 33% should be purchased by Central and State Government Departments/agencies
specially when the items reserved for SSI sector have been withdrawn and majority of the items have been put on OGL
list.  The policy of purchase preference system as followed by USA Government for protection of indigenous industries
may be emulated.  Necessary action in this regard should be initiated by the Ministry of SSI immediately.

XXIII.  PARTNERSHIP ACT
 
23.1     The representatives of   Laghu Udyog Bharati stated, “ In the entire Budget, no mention has been made about the
Partnership Act.  There are four ways in which I can start a business:  (1) Partnership (2) Proprietorship  (3) Limited

Ministry should take steps to provide such measures so as to enable the small entrepreneurs to use the facilities provided
by the incubators as they compete against importers as well as other domestic producers.

participation of state governments, NGOs and SSI Associations should be ensured by providing appropriate
encouragement to them. This is in keeping with the Industrial policy announced in 1991to give special thrust to the
promotion and strengthening of small tiny and village industries.

which have failed to make payment to SSIs in due time.   Necessary amendment for taking punitive   action may also
be   contemplated in the Delayed Payment Act.

The Committee recommends that adequate safeguards be bililt within to avoid such recurrence in
future,

Action Taken :

In the aftermath of Smelter debacle, several committees including one external finding
Committee were constituted. The Committee has broadly come to the conclusion that gradual
deterioration in the performance of pots over the years was mainly due to non-adherence to
standard operating practices, improper maintenance, poor werk culture, improper planning and
lack of team work. Based on the recommendations of the Committee. the following safeguards
were built within the system to avoid such failure in the future.

With a view to have effective utilization of manpower for a full eight hours, the gate
control system was reinforced with effect from 13.05.98 and workers in shifts are being retained
for the full eight hours, Workers are now being allotted sufficient work and more flexibility in
utilization of manpower has been enforced so that they are engaged in full shifts.

Commencing from Ist July, 1998, a system has been introduced to carry Out
inspection/surprise checking to check the attendance and physical presence of the employees
deployed in the respective shifts and mark absent those not found present in the place of work,

Instructions have been issued to implement the standard operating procedures,

The undeserved overtime has been completely stopped since 1st of July, 1998. A number
of committees headed by Dy, General Managers are inspecting different work areas to ascertain
the number of employees engaged on overtime, the reasons for such overtime, and the attendance
of the workmen during overtime hours, and, in case any of them is not found at work, spot they
are marked absent.

The incentive scheme has been revised. In the revised incentive scheme maximum
importance has been given to production and a cut off level of production has been provided
below which no incentive becomes payable to employees,

An effective strategy has been chalked out to enforce discipline, Any act of indiscipline is
being viewed seriously and action is being taken against the erring employees. Already three

Recommendations/Observation of the committee (Para 19,1)
Import Duty

The Committee recommends that the Government may consider enhancing the import
duty on such scraps to the same level as that of primary aluminium metal,

Action Taken Report

Enhancing the import duty on aluminium scrap would lessen its utilization, specially
when use of scrap is cost effective and energy efficient. Conversion of scrap into metal uses only
about 5% of the energy required to reduce alumina into metal, Moreover, recycling is
environmentally friendly as it does not release green house gases like CO2. Aluminium is also
fully recyclable, a process which can conserve a precious non-renewable resource like Bauxite.
For these reasons, about 30% of the global aluminium metal Production is scrap based, and the
duty on scrap is generally lower than that on primary metal. Since the use of scra,) is not
widespread in India, the Report of the Working Group on Non-ferrous Metals (Ninth Plan 1997-
2002), had specifically recommended that recycling of scrap requires less energy and is also
able to meet the gap between the domestic demand and supply. This can be achieved with import
of scrap. Thus, import needs to be promoted with low duty structure to make metal production
competitive. The global data on comparative customs duties does indicate that the duty on scrap
is generally lower, although there is not much difference in the tariffs on metal and scrap, the
tariffs on both being very low, both in deyeloped countries as well as in developing countries.
Keeping in view the above reasons, the Department of Mines had recommended to the Ministry
of Finance for low duty structure on import of aluminium scrap to make metal production
competitive (Union Budget 2002-2003). However, the basic import duty on aluminium serap has
been kept by Ministry of Finance at 15%.

Performance of  mineral maps
 
(Para 4.6) : The Committee is happy to note that IBM has taken up the task of  providing  the specialized and
Customized data, preparation of mineral maps and forest overlays. The Committee hopes that the IBM in tandem with
the Forest Survey of India and Ministry of Environment and Forest would continue to take up latest forest overlays
maps. Forest overlays maps used by State Government and Central Forest Department would help to cut-down delays in
obtaining forest clearance for Mining Lease ( ML ) and   prospective licence  (PL).
 
Action Taken 
: As per the decision taken by the National Advisory Committee on Environment aspects in Mining Areas
under the Chairmanship of Secretary (Mines) and Secretary (MOEF), 50 multi- mineral maps were completed by IBM
as per target of 2001-02 and sent to FSI for the forest overlays. The annual target for such maps for subsequent years has
been fixed  at 100 index maps on a scale1:50000. This activity is envisaged to cover entire mining area in the country
with the priority assigned to ecologically fragile area in the State of. Chattisgarh, Jharkhand, Orissa, Madhya Pradesh,
Karnataka  and   Rajasthan~ in line with the decision of MOEF.

Mines Control and conservation of Minerals Division (MCCM Division)
 
(Para 5.1.2): The Committee feels that MCCM division of IBM would be able to function effectively once IBM is made
a regulatory body because MCCM is entrusted with enforcement of systematic development of mineral deposits and
conservation studies.
 
Action Taken: There is a need for strict enforcement of MCDR, 1988 particularly in respect of small (B) category of
mines Special integrated studies covering 30-40 groups of mines in each region have been programmed to highlight the
issues involved in scientific mines on regional basis including  that of environmental aspects.

minerals throughout  the country .

wings of IBM may be well equipped for mineral beneficiation. The Sub-Committee further recommends that Ore
Dressing division of IBM should undertake such research work pertaining to beneficiation of low-Ore content mineral
in cost effective manner for viable and commercial production of metals.

Recommendations/Observations, which have been accepted by the Ministry of Mines :
 
Recommendations     (Para 3.2 )
 
Activities of  MECL
 
The Committee understands the vital  role of MECL in carrying out  detailed systematic mineral  exploration and hopes 
that  MECL  management  would be guided  by the management by objectives (MBO) and make its  earnest efforts for
achieving the cherished goals.
 
Action Taken
 
            The  observation of the  Committee has been noted.   MECL's  management is committed to  an overall
improvement of physico financial  performance of the company, to achieve the  goals set.
 
Recommendations        (Para 5.4)
 
Co-ordination and co-operation between MECL and GSI/Merger of MECL with GSI
 
The Committee is of the view that GSI should   undertake  honest effort for  searching and identifying   new prospects
for MECL for detailed exploration. 
 
Action Taken
 
MECL is in  constant touch with  GSI for identifying new prospects for obtaining detailed exploration work for the
company.
 
Recommendations     (Para 6.5)
 
Budgetary support
 
MNCs and private parties are doing exploration only for four  to  five precious and base etals and many other minerals
of national importance are still required to be  explored, which form a part of 64 minerals as mentioned in National
Mineral  inventory  of IBM, for which MECL  is the right choice.  Government should,  therefore,  continue budget
support to MECL.
 
Action Taken
 
            For  the year 2002-03 (BE),  Rs.8.00  crores has been provided  to MECL for promotional  projects which  is to
be reimbursed against work to be executed by  MECL.  Additional  funds  requirements.  if, any could be met out of the
Mineral Exploration Fund (MEF)  under which Rs.12.00  crores is also available
 
Recommendations     (7.3)
 
Performance of  MECL
 
The Committee appreciates the efforts made by MECL and hopes that it  would continue to strive its best in
implementing its programme of minerals exploration and mine development.
 
ACTION TAKEN
 
MECL  ensures to strive its best in implementing its programme of mineral exploration and mine development in  the 
country.  Customers satisfaction is  one of the key areas where the company needs to improve.  Under the ongoing

78th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/78threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:15:42]
liberalization process, it  is the endeavour of the company to obtain more contractual work from multi-national 
companies, both domestic and foreign, and execute the projects efficiently to meet their  requirements and remain
competitive.
 
Recommendation (8.4)
 
Physico-financial performance of MECL
 
The Committee is constrained to note that public sector support to MECL through promotion of  projects and
contractual work has considerably eroded.  The Committee feels that, if our PSUs are to remain, inter PSU cooperation
and synergy  is  required.
 
Action Taken
 
            To improve the physical performance of the company efforts are being made to get more jobs from PSUs and
State Government Organizations.  The Company has had detailed discussion with the officials of newly formed State of
Chattisgarh and Jharkhand to obtain work related to mineral explorations and development from these States.  In
addition, discussions have also been held with  UCIL, HCL, NMDC, AMD, SCCL, ONGC & CCL  for award of work
in the fields of mineral exploration mine development  and  IT enabled services.  MECL  management is hopeful to get
favourable results with constant persuasion with these and other organizations.
 
Recommendation       (15.3.2)
 
Coal sampling and analysis
 
            The Committee is pleased to note that MECL has  made its presence felt   in the   field  of coal sampling and
analysis.  The Committee  recommends  that MECL management should make effects for procuring work  order in this
field.
 
Action Taken
 
            For the year 2002-03 work order  for Rs. 250 lakhs  for coal sampling and analysis are available.  Though  in this
field a number of   private parties are also  active,  MECL is committed to grab each and every opportunity by  quoting
its most competitive  rates  to keep its resources and facilities created for the purposes gainfully deployed.
 
(Chapter - II)
 
Recommendations/Observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in view of the government’s
replies
 
Recommendations     (Para 4.4  )
 
Organisational Structure
 
            The Committee is of the view  that  zonal office should be made a profit making centre  and all projects assigned
to them should be in a such  a  way that each zonal office justifies is existence and each zonal office must   contribute in
the  profitability of  MECL .  The existence of zonal office  must contribute  in the profitability of MECL.  The
existence of zonal office  should  be linked to profitability.  The Committee further recommends that efforts should be
made  to reduce its administrative expenditure.
 
Action Taken
 
The Zonal offices are set up based on the availability of work.  Reduction in the availability of  work is  anticipated in

78th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/78threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:15:42]
2002-03.  Hence  the reduction  of  Zonal  offices   from  five to three   is being  contemplated.  The control of
expenditure vis-a-vis  the  availability of work is being exercised  strictly and the contribution towards profitability of
the company are being  monitored continuously.
 
Recommendation       (8.5)
 
Physical  and financial performance of MECL
 
            The Committee, while appreciating the physical performance of MECL, recommends that MECL management
should make efforts to  procure work orders from all concerned areas so that physical  performance of the  company
should have direct  positive impact on the financial performance of MECL.  The Committee hopes that once the
diversification programmes are implemented and financial restructuring proposals,  which is under the consideration of
Ministry of Finance, is approved and comes into effect, MECL would start making net profit.
 
 
Action Taken
 
MECL has been making  losses.  The gross sales  of the company has been mainly  on account of the work done for the
Government sector.  The company is dependent on equity,  loan and promotional grants.  Financial restructuring of the
company has been under the consideration of the  Government.   However, such an  exercise could be done only if the
company is able to remain viable on  a sustainable basis after such a process.  However, from the data presently
available it does not appear that financial restructuring would be viable.
 
 
Recommendation       ( 13.2)
 
SWOT analysis of MECL
 
The Committee understands that the strength of MECL is enough to be competitive in its activities and, therefore,   
recommends  that MECL  management  should take every  possible step to take advantage  of its strength and avail
opportunities to improve the financial and physical performance.  The Committee  further  recommends that MECL
management should make efforts for overcoming its weaknesses and imbibe sufficient and sustainable  resilience to
combat  threat to its existence.  MECL should also try  to  shed surplus work force under VRS.
 
Action Taken
 
MECL is committed to avail all opportunities in the field of Mineral Exploration and related activities with  its 
available resources and strength.   The  Company has diversified in areas such as Coal Bed  Methane (CBM)
exploration  and could make a break  through for drilling of slim holed on behalf  of ONGC.  It  has  successfully
completed the assigned job.  Based on the performance of MECL, ONGC  is considering award of additional work. 
Other organisations like  Reliance Industries, ESSAR, etc.  have approached MECL.  Simultaneously, the company has
been reducing its manpower  position.  Against the approved strength of 2500, it has 2586  employees on roll as on
1.4.02.  The Company proposes to  further reduce  its staff strength by 500.
 
Recommendation       (15.4.2)           
 
Mining & Beneficiation of Beach sand
 
            The Committee recommends that Government may grant the  lease at the earliest.
 
Action Taken
 
            Mining Lease of mineral sand at Tirunelveli, Tamil Nadu is in  advanced stage of consideration at the level of
State Government and is likely to be granted in  favour of MECL.  shortly.

Recommendation       (5.5)
 
Co-ordination and co-operation between MECL and GSI/Merger of MECL with GSI
 
            The Ministry of Mines may explore the possibility of merger of MECL with  Geological Survey of India (GSI) 
for better co-ordination and continued prospect for MECL for detailed exploration.  MECL could work as a separate
division in GSI structure.
 
Action Taken
 
            MECL had earlier   been a part of  GSI  and had been carved  out  of the  latter  in  1972 to undertake  detailed
exploration work.  Moreover, GSI as an organization, is itself in the process of revamping.
 
Further recommendation       (5.5)
 
Budgetary support
 
            The Committee is of the view that the Department of  Mines  should have furnished the details  of   GSI's
revamping  process and the extent  and  scope for co-operation and collaboration between GSI and MECL.  It is
because  of the fact that  MECL has been  covered out of GSI and  keeping in view the need to rationalise non-plan
expenditure through rightsizing manpower  and avoiding double set up  of administration, the  Committee recommended
merger of MECL with GSI.  At least MECL could be made a division of GSI while  discharging its present functions
and responsibility.   Such measures would not only lead to rationalisation of non-plan expenditure and avoidable
administrative expenditure, but would also strengthen both GSI and MECL.
 
Recommendation       (10.3)
           
Revival plan of MECL
 
Financial Restructuring
 
The Committee is of the view that implementation of the recommendations of the Revival Committee would have a
positive impact on the physical and financial performance of MECL.  The revival  committee had  recommended the 
writing off  of accumulated losses and waiver of interest on Government  loan to clean the balance sheet of  MECL.   
The Committee recommends that the request of MECL for  waiving  of the interest on loan and transfer of balance loan
amount to  equity should be considered by the Government so that MECL could make a turnaround .  The Department 
of Mines may seriously pursue the matter with the Ministry of Finance.
Action Taken
 
 
            MECL has been making  in losses.   The gross sales of the company has been mainly on account of the work 
done for the Government  sector.  The company is  dependent on equity, loan and promotional grants.  Financial
restructuring of  the  company has been under  the consideration of the Government.  However, such an exercise  could
be done only if the company is able to remain viable on a sustainable basis after such a process.  However, from the data
presently available it does not appear that financial restructuring would be viable.  The matter is presently under the
consideration of the Department of Mines.
 
Further recommendation       (10.3)

The Committee is constrained  to express  its concern over the reluctant approach of Department of Mines in regard to
future  prospects of MECL.  On the one hand   Department of Mines is indifferent  to the view of  merger  of MECL
with its parent body i.e.  GSI for injecting  a new  lease of life.  On the other hand,  the Department of Mines in not
convinced of MECL's capacity/resilience  to become viable even after implementation of financial  restructuring.  The
MECL's  proposal of financial restructuring   is gathering  dust in the Department of Mines.  This is a paradoxical state
of  affairs and speaks of inaction of the Department of Mines.  It seems that the Department  of Mines is banking on the
idea  that the things  would improve automatically  without  any efforts/measures  while  the fact of the situation is that
MECL's proposal of financial restructuring needs immediate aid from the Government to make the company sustainable
on a regular basis. Therefore, the Committee recommends that the Department of Mines must come out of its slumber
and act promptly in pushing ahead the financial restructuring proposals of MECL.
 
Recommendation       (11.6)
 
Grant of PL and ML
 
            The Committee is happy to note that MECL is making efforts towards obtaining prospecting licence and mining
lease.  The Committee   recommends that PL and ML may be granted, notwithstanding, the  Disinvestments proposal. 
MECL should be allowed to show its mettle.
 
Action Taken
 
            MECL has been applying for prospecting and mining leases  from State Governments.  MECL has applied for
mining lease  for Mineral Sand deposits in Tirunelveli District in  Tamil Nadu.  The Company is expected  to sign an
MOU shortly with the State Government  for setting up a Titanium Dioxide plant in the state   before grant of ML.   It
is   expected  that ML will  be granted in MECL’s favour.
 
Further recommendation
 
            In  Action Taken  Note to this present report the MECL management   should  furnish the outcome of  action 
taken in regard to the fate of application   for obtaining  prospecting  licence (PL) and Mining lease (ML) .
 
 
 
Recommendation       ( 12.3)
 
Research and Development activities of MECL
 
            The Committee is of the opinion that MECL  should  prepare technological  road maps exploring its
opportunities and understanding technological road blocks for innovative technological break through.  The Committee
is of  the view  that the MECL should  set up a R&D Wing for undertaking R&D  projects in order to attain leadership
in its spheres of activities.  It  may be noted  that technological leadership is a product of vision, innovation, experiment
coming out of research  work.  MECL  may contribute  in developing   technology  and skill in detailed exploration.
 
Action Taken
 
            The Research and Development activities  in the  area of detailed exploration  are   being  taken up to be at par
with other exploration companies.
 
Further recommendation:
 
            The Committee reiterates its recommendation  that MECL  management should set up   an R&D wing in MECL
for undertaking  R&D project in  order to  attain  leadership in its spheres of activities.  MECL, if it once attains
technological leadership in the field of detailed  exploration, it may not only prove a  milestone in its way of revival but

78th Report
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/78threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:15:42]
well undertake steps for  technology export  in the field detailed exploration  to other developing countries.
 
Recommendation       (15.1.3)
           
Business Plan of MECL
 
The  Committee is happy to observe that MECL is emerging as one of the leading agencies in the field of CBM 
exploration.   As the  Government of India  has also  liberalized  the CBM   policy  recently and seven CBM blocks has
been auctioned, and association of MECL with prospective.  Indian/foreign  entrepreneurs will go a long way in
developing the CBM resources.  MECL should not leave any stone unturned in getting orders for exploration. 
Government also should give priority of  MECL.
 
Action Taken
 
             MECL  has already identified  plant  and machinery as well as trained  manpower to undertake slim hole drilling
for development of CBM resources in the country.  The company has been making all out efforts to get the work orders
for  exploration  of CBM from the agencies associated in this field.  It is expected that with the final  allocation of CBM 
blocks to the various agencies, MECL would be able to provide its services on most competitive basis to the satisfaction
of the clients.
 
Further recommendation:
 
            The Committee is of the view that MECL  management should continue  its all out efforts  for getting the work 
orders for exploration of  Coal Bed Methane (CBM) from the agencies  associated in the field.  The Committee further 
recommends that the Development  of Mines should extend its all possible to assistance to MECL management  in their
efforts   for procuring  work order.  The committee desires that the Department of Mines should furnish in the ATN  of
present report the details of efforts undertaken on the   part of MECL  management (names of agencies with whom
MECL management  interacted and  their response),  assistance extended by the Department of Mines, in this regard and
the overall outcome of efforts undertaken in the   form  of quantum of work order received  by MECL management in
the  field of CBM.
 
Recommendation (15.5.3)
 
Ground Water exploration
 
            The Committee  understands that  effective utilization is essential for proper water planning and  management. 
The Committee feels  that MECL with its rich experience in deep drilling and exploration, should  be able to play a
positive role in exploring ground water  which is gradually becoming a  scarce resource.
 
Action Taken
 
            MECL with its experience  in deep  drilling considered  ground water exploration as a new field for 
diversification.   However, MECL's board  is of the opinion that there is  severe competition in  the market for ground
water exploration and, therefore, it has been deferred for the time  being.
 
Further recommendation      (15.5.3)
 
            The Committee is of the view that  MECL  should   come out with an all out effort in the  field of ground water 
and should not be deterred  by competition.   Therefore, the Committee expects that MECL management would give due
impetus to the drilling and exploration of ground water.

Recommendations        (Para 7.3)
MANPOWER OF HCL
Rationalisation of manpower   is  an essential   factor for running  any company in profit.  HCL management should
further  rationalise manpower to the extent possible  in all of its units so that cost -component  of manpower in all HCL
units should conform to  the overall cost  benefit analysis.   Government  may review the  VRS  requirement and  fulfill 
it as early as possible.
Action Taken
During last three, the Government has provided a non plan loan of Rs.440 Crore for VRS. 8373 employees have been
separated by VRS. VRS requirement has been further reviewed and it is planned to separate 3000 employees on VRS
for which the Government proposes to make the funds available as  a grant and a restructuring proposal to that effect has
been submitted and considered by CCEA.
Recommendations        (Para 15.3)
MALANJKHAND COPPER PROJECT
Production performance
The Sub-Committee has been  given to  understand  that MCP is a  prospective  plant of HCL  and hopes that  MCP
would achieve the target of production  of copper metal in concentrate  (MIC)  during the year 2001-2002 .
Action Taken
The production of metal in concentrate in MCP during 2001-02 was 24,085 tonnes. Hence, the target was achieved.
Recommendations (Para : 16.3)
Production Cost
The  Committee notes that the progressive increase in the  production cost of   metal in concentrate  is mainly due to
increase in interest burden and administrative expenditure  on Head Quarter.  The  Committee  strongly recommends
that HCL should   take   steps in right earnest for rationalisation /reduction in administrative expenditure so that  MCP 
would be able to run without  much losses.
Action Taken
The company has taken various steps to reduce its interest burden and administrative expenditure on Head Quarter.
High cost term loan of Rs.150 crore taken from IDBI, bearing interest rate of 16% ,has been with issue of bonds with
interest 10.65% per annum. This has resulted in savings of Rs. 8 crores per annum.
Recommendations        (Para 18.3)
MANPOWER  OF MCP
The Committee appreciates the efforts taken by MCP management  towards rationalisation of manpower because 
optimum manpower is a pre-requisite condition for  reducing the cost of production.  The Sub-Committee notes the 
strategic  restructuring of manpower in MCP off-loading  of ancillary services and re-deployment  of existing manpower
in production sector.  This is a  step  in right direction.  With this the Committee hopes MCP would be able to improve
its condition considerably.
Action Taken
The Committee's appreciation for rationalisation of manpower and off loading of ancillary services at MCP is noted.
Recommendations        (Para 22.4)
SUPPORT NEEDED FROM THE GOVERNMENT
The Committee understands that the  basic  transportation  and  communication facilities are   essential for    running
any plant in profits.  The Committee feels that the Department of Mines should have  acted as facilitator   to improve 
basic  infrastructure.  The role of the Department of Mines is found wanting in this regard.  However, the Committee
recommends that the   Department of Mines should now take up the matter with State Government for improving the
road condition linking MCP ensuring conducive procurement of essential inputs and for transportation of   its finished

Recommendations
 
CAPITAL RESTRUCTURING (Para : 3.7)
The Committee is constrained  to express  its concern over the adverse business prospects of Hindustan copper Ltd due
to weak financial base of the company which   continued to work long   on  unviable mines .  The Company is  in deep   
troubles  and is  heading towards a  point of no return.  Its  operation might come to a standstill if  concrete steps  are not
