competitiveness, meeting technical requirements, adherence to reasonable qualification criteria etc., especially in case of
International Competitive Bidding (ICB) tenders. These are hallmarks of today's business environment in the opened up
economy where public sectors not covered under administered price regime have to compete with Indian private sector and
multinational companies at times even on unequal footing. Therefore, as a pre-requisite, any inter-PSE cooperation has to
have a directive from the centre and a mandate for being operational and successful.
27.2Most of the public sector enterprises in the industrial field were created for catering to the infrastructure  needs of the
country where investment from private sector was not forthcoming. As such, if at all there is going to be any structured inter-
PSE cooperation, it should cover all the areas of infrastructure etc. by utilizing their synergies rather than catering to only the
inter-PSE needs in the engineering and construction sectors.
27.3With the opening up of the Indian economy, sectoral policies are no more seamlessly linked and every company has to
compete with every other company for getting business in India as well as abroad. In this scenario inter-PSE cooperation
should be directed by a Government policy framework on the subject which should ensure that policy pronouncements and
their implementation are beyond the purview of WTO provisions but also competition law, which is equally applicable to
PSEs, may also come in the way of mutual cooperation unless validated by a national policy framework.
27.4However, inter PSE cooperation for maximizing the business among public sector units and utilizing the assets created at
great cost to the country is a desirable objective at the national level, which will have positive impact on the economy. While
ensuring that this objective is realised, it is also necessary that the PSEs be enabled to become competitive, for which a policy
framework should be in place to ensure availability of critical inputs such as technology flows, which are particularly
necessary for PSEs in the engineering and construction sectors.
27.5Suggestions to improve the viability of PSUs
l     PSUs should form a consortium or enter into a joint venture partnerships to exploit their potential strength in the
best manner so that they can compete with MNCs.
l     There should be central coordination committee to guide and encourage PSUs to pull up their resources and form
consortium.
l     There should be a central coordination committee to bring together buyer as well as seller PSUs across the table to
sort out their issues/disputes.
l     There should be an overseeing mechanism and laid down policy to stop duplication of foreign collaborations for
similar products by different PSUs.
l     Since the large infrastructure is not fully utilized, purchase preference should continue.
l     Dealings amongst the PSUs Should be more transparent and documents resulting to decision by one accessible to
the other.
27.6Authorising MDs of MoU signing PSUs to approve overseas tour programmes of the functional Directors
27.7Based on Cabinet approval, DPE had agreed to authorise MDs of MoU-signing-PSUs to approve overseas tour
programme of the functional Directors. Subsequently, on the instructions from the Ministry of Heavy Industry, the DPE had
withdrawn these powers with the result that proposals for overseas visits of even functional directors of all PSUs have to be
sent for minister's approval.
27.8More than 50 per cent of IRCON's annual business comes from overseas operations. It is to be appreciated that IRCON
basically contracts the company and clients are required to discuss urgent contract projects related issues with the top
management of the contract or company at a very short notice of 2-3 days. The normal procedure of obtaining approval from
the concerned Minister takes anything from two to three weeks, with the result that it becomes embarrassing to explain to the
client about delay in coming for meeting/discussion.
27.9It is therefore suggested that while tour programmes of MDs of MoU signing companies may still be approved by the
concern Minister, authority of MDs in MoU signing PSUs to approve overseas program of the functional directors should be
restored at the earliest so as to remove this handicap.
Observation on Purchase Preference
27.10 From the above background it is absolutely clear that the very aim of the Government to implement the philosophy of
purchase preference in the true spirit is defeated when more than one PSU bidders participate for a job, since the situation
leads to competition amongst the bidding PSUs undercutting each other and possibly submitting cost ineffective proposals.
Even if there is one PSU bidder for a particular job, and PSU customers prepared to give a purchase preference to the bidding
PSUs, in absence of the proper level playing field, it sometimes becomes impossible for the bidding PUSs to match the price
of L1 bidders in the private sector. In fact, in tender enquiries of PSU customers, more often do not mention purchase
preference clause. Not only this, bid qualify and consequent requirements framed in such a way e.g. minimum turnover
figures and profitability for three consequent financial years prior to bid submission date etc. match, i.e., some PSU bidders

27.11 To the entire background and philosophy of setting up of various PSUs several years back as compared to many private
sector companies and multinationals, who had very definite advantages of entering the field later need to be pragmatically

Global Tenders
27.12 Many of the major PSUs particularly in coal and power sector had been issuing global tenders even for range of the
equipments that are available indigenously with established manufacturing and product support/service facilities and the
products are already established with purchaser PSU for a long time. Even though such global tenders may provide for
purchase preference to central PSUs, the following anomalies still exist which require to be addressed to for providing level
playing field and implementing the govt. policy in letter and spirit.
(a)   Price preference of 15%: against all global tenders, MNCs are eligible to participate and this amounts to
international competitive bidding. In such ICB where purchases financed by multilateral agencies like IBRD, ADB
etc. bids offering the goods manufactured in the purchaser's country with minimum 30% value addition on ex-works
price quoted and that production facility has been extended at least since the date of bid submission and considered
under group 'A' category. The fully imported offers are considered under group 'C' category. For the bids under 'A'
category, there are domestic price preferences of 15% on CIF value of imported goods (amount of customs duty and
other import tax that a non-exempt importer would have to pay for importation of goods offered under 'C' category or
15% of CIF value of goods offered, whichever is low) in evaluation. If group 'A' of domestic bidder thus becomes L1
in evaluation, after considering 15% price preference, group 'A' domestic bidder will not get contract at the bid price
quoted. This facility of 15% price preference to indigenous goods evaluation is not available in respect of global
tenders, where competition will be from international bidders, same in line with World Bank tenders. This facility of
15% price preference is to be extended by Government of India to all global tenders.
28.   Bid Currencies
28.1In IBRD and ADB tenders, indigenous bidders are allowed to quote in foreign currency also and are paid in currency
quoted. This is not being allowed in domestic and global bids and indigenous manufacturers are asked to quote price in
rupees only, whereas in case of imported offer evaluation is done by converting the foreign currency bids into Indian Rupees
at the exchange rate, as applicable on the date of bid opening; the actual outgo will be at the rate as applicable on the date of
payment against shipments though L/C.
28.2Hence domestic bidders particularly where import content is substantial (meeting the minimum value addition of 30 pc)
should be allowed to quote in foreign currency also for import content and subject to same type of evaluation as applied in
fully imported equipment. Payment should also be made to domestic bidders for the foreign currency portion in equivalent
rupees, at the exchange rate applicable on the date of supply, without asking for further confirmation on documents.
29.   Special Additional Duty
29.1As per policy, SAD is applied at 4% on all imports and the same is non-MOD vatable. In the case of indigenous offer,
particularly where the value of import content is high, SAD is paid on import content and in addition, CST is also charged at
4% on the ex-factory price plus FD. Thus, indigenous offers will be in a disadvantageous position when compared to the
imported offer in total evaluation to the extent of CST.
        The following points need consideration
(a)     Purchase preference to be given for domestic offers onIy between established non-PSE sector and established
PSE sector including joint ventures in the later case, subject to value addition being minimum 30%.
(b)   In case of global tenders, domestic bidders should be given 15% preference as allowed in the case of
international competitive bidding, in addition to purchase preference.
(c)   Domestic bidders to be allowed to quote in foreign currency plus Indian Rupees when import content is of a
high value and payments to be made by purchasing PSE to selling PSE in equivalent Indian Rupees, for
corresponding foreign exchange value at the exchange rate as applicable on the date of supplies.
(d)   Purchase policy is to be extended for another three years that is up to 31st March 2005.
(e)   All tenders issued by the central PSUs and Government departments (central and state) for goods and services
of more than one crore value should incorporate purchase preference clause strictly in line with the government
guidelines and extend the same to a bids offered by selling PSUs as mandatory.
(f)    In case of global tenders, the tender document should contain 15% price preference in evaluation and if
domestic central PSE offer becomes L1 with this price preference, the order should be placed on the central
PSE at the quoted price.
29.2Exemption to PSUs should be given from submission of Earnest Money deposit. In lieu of draft/cash/B.G., PSUs should
be allowed to submit indemnity bond.

CHAPTER-IV
OBSERVATIONS/FINDINGS OF THE COMMITTEE
 
30.1The Committee, while having interaction with the PSUs, considered it proper to take a view on the following points
offered by various PSUs:
(i)    Cooperation in defence and railway sectors
        The possibility of partnership in manufacturing defence equipment with Ordnance Factory Board and with RITES
and other railway  organisations for railways equipment, locomotive should be explored.          
(ii)    Cooperation in infrastructure sector
        PSUs in the infrastructure sector should join hands and deliver a project to the satisfaction of the customer within
reasonable qualifying conditions. The provision of joint bidding may be explored.
(iii)   Approval of sub-vendor
        Many client PSUs  including  SEBs   specify their own vendors for procurement of certain equipment and also
prescribe approval of sub-vendors. This condition often works to the detriment of the PSUs. The job of appointment
of sub-vendors should be left with the main supplier PSU.           
(iv)   Cooperation in risk sharing
        There is a need for increased cooperation among the client and supplier  PSUs in terms of provisions such as
suitable risk sharing in respect of penalty clauses as well as field trial of new products developed etc.                
(v)   Development of products linked to a single dominant customer
        PSUs which developed products linked to a single dominant PSU and made long term fixed investment in
equipment technology, manpower etc. do not get to realise adequate returns due to sudden drop in order inflow.
This is the area where a study is required for the survival of supplier PSUs.  DPE should find out which are the
PSUs that are affected by such sudden drop of  orders.
(vi)   Making PSUs truly board-managed companies
        PSUs are not truly Board-managed as in the private sector. In the present business scenario, there is a need to
expedite the process of transformation of PSUs to autonomous  Board-managed companies so that the need of
purchase preference can be obviated.    
(vii)  Central coordination committee and buyers’ and sellers’ meet
        There should be a central coordination committee to guide and encourage PSUs to form a consortium or join
venture to exploit their potential strength in the best manner so that they can compete with the MNCs.  This
committee should also bring together buyer as well as seller PSUs across the table to sort out their issues/disputes
for settlement outside the arbitration. The committee would also review and establish proper education of
collaborative approach between and among PSUs and arrange Buyers and sellers meet.
(viii)Preventing duplication of foreign collaboration for similar products
        There have been cases where foreign collaboration was sought by the PSUs for similar products. There should be a
mechanism for information dissemination so that duplication of such activities can be avoided.
(ix)   Unutilised infrastructure
        Huge infrastructure created in pre-liberalised era is lying unutilised or partially utilised due to lack of orders. In
cases where the PUSs have been closed due to various reasons, their assets are also lying unutilised. Government
should come forward with a proposal for best utilisation of unutilised/partially utilised/under-utilised infrastructure
to prevent unauthorised encroachment by the antisocial elements.
(x)   Customs duty on re-import of machinery
        
The Indian projects exporters temporarily export some construction equipment from India for a particular project
abroad and on its completion, may shift the same to another project, either in the same or another country and
finally it is brought back to India after project is implemented. Such re-import attracts customs duty even though no

export benefit may have been availed at the time of export. This needs to be addressed.
(xi)   Attractive Voluntary Retirement Scheme
        Voluntary Retirement Scheme should be such as can reasonably be expected to enable an employee to make a new
beginning in life. But the Income Tax Rules and Government guidelines have failed to draw response to the scheme.
The PSUs should be allowed to frame more liberalised VRS to make it attractive. For this purpose, provision of
Income Tax Rules including upper ceiling of Rs.5 lakhs should be suitably modified. Budgetary support should also
be provided for the purpose.
(xii)  Foreign Tour
        DPE has withdrawn the power of MDs of MoU signing PSUs to approve the overseas tour of functional Directors.
This has created Difficulty when the PSU has to discuss contract project related issues with the  management of a
foreign company at a very short notice of 2-3  days as the approval of the concerned Minister comes after 2-3 weeks
and it becomes embarrassing to explain to the foreign client about the delay in coming for the meeting. DPE should
address the issue and sort out the problem.
(xiii)Combining of Synergies
        Some of the big PSUs and small PSUs are manufacturing similar products. In the post-liberalised era, existing
synergies of big and small PSUs should be combined to bring a better result. For example, Engineering & Electrical
Divisions of AYCL and BHEL have can non synergies and their synergies can be combined to achieve a fruitful
result. DPE should make a study of the matter and submit a status note to the Committee.
(xiv)Coordination with the Ministry of Railways
        Ministry of railways can play a vital role in implementing the concept of inter-PSU  cooperation. DPE should
initiate a dialogue with the Ministry of railways for allotment of railway equipments to PSUs under the control of
various administrative ministries. A   step in this regard would definitely usher in a new era in revitalising the PSUs.
(xv)  15%Price Preference
        In case of global tenders, domestic bidders should be given 15% price preference as allowed in the case of
international Competitive Bidding.  The Sub-Committee is separately examining this matter for the Capital Goods
Industry. DPE  may examine its application to other sectors of the industry.
1.     Bid in foreign currency
        Domestic bidders to be allowed to quote in foreign currency plus Indian Rupee when import content is of high
value and payments to be made by purchasing PSU to selling PSU in equivalent rupees, for corresponding
foreign exchange value at the exchange rate as applicable on the date of supplies. DPE should sort out the
matter in consultation with the concerned authority.
2.     Reasonable pre-qualification criteria
        Sometimes PSUs stipulate pre-qualification criteria, which Indian bidders then with good capability can not
match. DPE should  find out, which PSUs are stipulating unreasonable PQ criteria so that greater outflow to
foreign contractor is stopped. This is especially relevant in LSTK  projects.
3.     Past track record- negative net worth
        PSUs  individually or in consortium can   implement various infrastructure projects. But the bid qualification
with respect to past record (negative net worth) many times does not permit the PSUs even to pre-qualify. The
pre-qualification criterion should be relaxed to facilitate their  participation. DPE  should examine the matter in
consultation with the concerned PSUs under the control of various ministries.
4.     World Bank guideline in respect of wagon procurement
        Container  Corporation of India is mainly  purchasing  wagons financed by loans sanctioned by the World
Bank. The procurement of wagons has therefore to be done within the procurement guidelines issued by the
World Bank and in these guidelines there is no provision for purchase preference for products and
manufactures by the PSUs. DPE should examine whether the above procurement comes under the 15%  price 
preference to domestic companies under the World Bank guidelines. In case it is covered by the World Bank
guidelines, the PSEs may jointly or in consortium of private domestic sector bid for supply of wagons.
5.     Release of Liquidated Damages
        Sometimes client PSUs impose liquidated damages on supplier PSU due to delay in supply of products. This
results in stoppage of flow of much  needed cash to the supplier PSUs. Liquidated Damages should be released

where delay has not affected the overall completion schedule of the project.
        DPE should make an exercise in this regard in coordination with the Department of Programme 
Implementation.                
6.     Indemnity Bond
        Between two PSUs the requirement of bank  guarantees may be waived and Indemnity Bond may be accepted
for saving in the bank charges as also help the PSUs in case of  bank limit problems. DPE should explore the
possibilities of introducing such a system.
7.     Research and Development Unit in the PSUs
        The PSUs have to continuously improve their technology and quality levels for making their products
acceptable to the customers. For this purpose R&D units should be set up in each and every PSU and
weightage on R&D facilities should be given in MoUs signed by the PSUs with their administrative ministries.
8.     Amendment of Contract Labour Law
        Amendment of Contract Labour Law, 1970 would help in a big way to resolve the corporate activities, which
are totally labour-oriented. DPE should take up the matter with the Ministry of Labour.
9.     Purchase from PSUs
        Out side the Purchse Preference Policy, all the PSUs autonomous bodies should purchase certain part of total
annual purchase from the PSUs eligible to supply.
25.   Emphasis on Quality
        The Committee  observes that utmost emphasis should be given on the quality of product. The PSUs should
help each other without compromising the quality and competitive spirit. The Department of Public Enterprise
should play a pro-active role in the matter for helping the PSUs. Hitherto. DPE’s role has not been that pro-
active as it should have been. Detractors of PSUs in government circle may come forward with the reasoning
that inter-PSU cooperation is not necessary as PSUs are likely to be disinvested. In defence of mutual
cooperation among PSUs it may be said that by such cooperation the PSUs will be strengthened, and it will
fetch better price in the eventually of their privatisation.
26.   Impetus to Shipping Industry
1.     Indian  shipping  companies  should  place  orders  on  Hindustan  Shipyard Ltd. to utilise the shipbuilding
facilities;
2.     ONGC should place orders for construction of offshore platforms,  since an exclusive platform fabrication
yard  was created for ONGC;
3.     Shipping companies should send their vessels for repair at Hindustan Shipyard Dry Dock to utilise the
infrastructure optimally.
27.   Unreasonable Prequalification stipulated by PSUs
        The Committee recommends that there should be a mechanism in DPE through which it should be possible to
refer such unreasonable pre-qualifications stipulated by certain PSUs. In many cases  Indian bidders with good
capability cannot be even with suitable foreign break-up.  Such restrictions stifle growth opportunities for
Indian firms, curb their initiative and lead to greater outflow to foreign contractors.
28.
  The Committee therefore recommends that Department of Public Enterprises should initiate action in respect of
all the above points of this report and appoint a Task Force to implement these points in the best possible
manner. The Committee also observed that presently there is existence of permanent Machinery of Arbitration
for reassertion of differences in the Department of Public Enterprises. However, no positive progress in this
direction exists. The Committee recommends setting up a Take Force for a positive thrust towards PSU
coordination having representative sample of client and service PSUs/Departments with the position of the
chairman being tenure based, by rotation to be filled by election. The task force shall submit periodic reports to
this Committee/parliament in significant initiations and important achievements on a periodic  basis. The
Committee understands that the task entrusted to DPE is not a small one and requires monumental effort but the
committee hopes that the Department will leave no stone unturned to  bring the PSUs out of woods.

BACKGROUND
1.         Khadi and Village Industries have the unique capacity to generate large employment opportunities in the rural
areas at a low capital cost and hence occupy an important place in the national economy. These industries develop local
initiatives, cooperation and spirit of self-reliance in the economy and at the same time help in utilization of available
manpower for processing locally available raw materials by adoption of simple techniques.
1.1       Prior to Independence, the development of Khadi and Village Industries was entirely a non-governmental effort
under the inspired guidance of Mahatma Gandhi. After Independence, the Government of India assumed responsibility
of bringing development of Khadi and Village Industries within the overall framework of the Five Year Plans and set up
the Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC) by an Act of Parliament in 1956. In the year 1987-88, the
Government of India, as per the recommendations of the Khadi and Village Industries Review Committee (KAVIRC),
amended the KVIC Act, which ushered in considerable expansion of the scope of village industries making it eligible
for KVIC finance and coverage. KVIC now plays pivotal role in the strengthening of rural economy by providing
employment opportunities by promotion of Khadi and Village Industries.
1.2       One of the principal objectives of the KVIC is to promote non-farm employment opportunities in rural areas.
The Committee understands that KVIC has been able to generate full time as well as subsidiary occupation to the rural
people. A major chunk of these beneficiaries are from the weaker sections of the society, such as women, SC/STs,
minorities etc., which reflects the acceptability of KVI programme for the betterment of weaker sections in rural areas.
About 40 per cent of employment generated under KVI Sector goes in favour of rural women. Another important
feature of KVI programme is the large coverage of SC/ST artisans/entrepreneurs. The coverage of SC/ST artisans in the
employment generated under KVI programme is as high as 34 per cent. KVIC implements its programmes through 30
States/UT level Khadi and Village industries boards, 5599 registered institutions, 30,138 cooperative societies and 8.43
lakh individuals and about 7500 exclusive sales outlets throughout the country.
1.3       Khadi is an activity committed for the upliftment of the poor. It provides supplementary employment to enhance
their income in spare time and that too at their doorsteps. Most of the women spinners spin only after completing their
household chores. Thus it helps in maintaining their family life undisturbed. This is very important from the social point
of view too. When a women goes out of house for job, naturally, the next generation suffers for want of due care. This
drawback of industrialization is avoided here.

2.3       During the course of its visit the Committee found that state KVIB performance was not satisfactory. It showed
no 'A' or 'B' category institution to mark its impact. Further, the number of institutions monitored by it was only two
against 12 institutions monitored by KVIC.
2.4       The Committee observes that in order to identify the drawbacks in the functioning of the Khadi
institutions and to take timely remedial measures, KVIC should closely monitor Khadi institutions under various
categories like A, B, C and D especially those institutions whose functioning is not at the desired level. KVIC
should ensure decentralization in decision making and delegation of more powers to State KVIB alongwith
development of a strong monitoring system.
INITIATIVES  TAKEN  FOR  ENHANCING  KHADI  SALES
2.5       The Committee was apprised that a meeting was convened by KVIC with all the institutions under this Region to
enhance the sales of the Khadi by conducting the sale outside the Bhandars, undertaking mobile sales, hawking sales at
important places, main roads of the towns/cities. The representatives were requested to participate in the Khadi
exhibition-cum-sales at Guntur and other Fashion shows. A fashion show cum sales was organized at Rajahmundry with
NGOs and East Godavari District Khadi and Rural Development Samatha, Kakinada.
2.6       The Committee observes that Khadi sales pick up only when rebate is offered to the customers. Sans
rebate, Khadi sales have shown downward trend during the year. The Committee recommends that KVIC
should encourage individual entrepreneurs to sell Khadi products on commission basis. There should also be
attempt to make the Khadi products cheaper, qualitatively better and market competitive.

3.         Karnataka State is one of the pioneering States in the country producing quality khadi. Some of the important
khadi products produced in the State are cotton khadi, National Flag of Garag, silk khadi of Kolar and Mysore District,

implementation of Khadi Programme, out of which, 58 institutions are working. Under KVIB fold, out of 144 aided

3.1       The Committee observes that Karnataka has the potential of producing speciality goods like National Flag of
Garage, silk khadi of Kolar and Mysore, muslin of Bizapur which are unique. There is huge potential of export of these
products. The Committee recommends that KVIC should promote district/regional level village industry federations
consisting of artisans, district listed institutions and margin money beneficiaries.

KVIC has established a "Central Silver Plant" at Chitradurga during the year 1992-93. The CSP supplies the quality

and Village Industries Sector in the State. The Board has shown remarkable progress in all the schemes assigned to it by
both the State and Central Governments. Certain issues relating to Khadi and Village Industries Sector, require
attention. The issues are :

(i)         Extending Margin Money Scheme for opening exclusive KVI Retail Sales Outlets :
3.5       The Committee observes that Margin Money Scheme is at present being extended for establishing
Industries, Business and Service ventures mainly in rural areas. This has resulted in creation of large capacities
in production side without much support in marketing of products produced. Therefore, it is necessary to create
forward linkages by supporting and assisting in marketability of the products. The Committee recommends that
exclusive KVI retail sales outlets in urban and semi-urban areas should be opened by extending Margin Money
assistance. If necessary, waiver of rural criteria as in the case of leather units should be done in which exemption
is available to those leather units as are located in rural areas.
(ii)        Extension of Interest Subsidy Eligibility Certificate to the units established under CBC and Margin
Money Scheme :
3.6       The interest subsidy scheme is being in force for almost two decades. This scheme is not extended to the
units established under CBC and Margin Money Scheme. There are quite a good number of units like Rice Mills,
Dal Mills, Rava Mills, Stone Cutting and Polishing etc., which require huge working capital for the viability. In
all these cases, the Committee observes the only one cycle requirement of working capital, has been provided
with the presumption that units should avail remaining working capital from the Banks. The Committee,
therefore, recommends that interest subsidy eligibility certificate should be extended to the units established
under CBC and Margin Money Scheme.
(iii)       Modernization of Cotton Khadi Production Centres :
3.7       The Committee came to know that a proposal has been prepared for modernization of cotton khadi
production centres in Karnataka. This proposal envisages conversion of 1125 charkhas from the present 6
spindles to 8 spindles charkhas. The estimated cost of the proposal is Rs. 101.25 lakhs towards capital
expenditure i.e., replacement of 6 spindle charkha by 8 spindle charkha and Rs. 54.64 lakhs interest subsidy on
working capital to be borrowed from the financial institutions/banks. The Committee observes that the
modernization of cotton khadi production centres will improve the productivity of Khadi Institutions and khadi
artisans will be able to earn increased wages due to increased production. The Committee, therefore,
recommends that proposal submitted to KVIC should be examined and the required amount under budgetary
sources should be sanctioned without delay.

4.         The Committee was, however, apprised that at the time of inception of the Margin Money Scheme, the KVI
Board was permitted by the KVIC to implement the scheme uniformly through Cooperative Banks, Nationalized Banks,
Private Sector Scheduled Banks, Regional Rural Banks and the Kerala Financial Corporation. But in July, 2000 the
Commission unilaterally modified the procedure and accorded sanction to the Board to operate the scheme only with the
specific approval of the Commission. Subsequently the Commission accorded specific approval to the Board to
implement the scheme through all the implementing agencies except Kerala Financial Corporation. The approval in
respect of Kerala Financial Corporation is pending with the Commission for a long time even though the Board has
made available all the documents required by the Commission for the specific approval. It is reliably learnt that the
Industrial Development Bank of India has raised some objection to allow the State Financial Corporation to advance
loans to the beneficiaries under the Margin Money Scheme and this has posed a serious problem to the Board. Due to
the non-receipt of approval to the Kerala Financial Corporation the Board is not in a position to provide Margin Money
Assistance to 101 applications to the tune of Rs. 2.21 crore cleared by Kerala Financial Corporation.
4.1       The Committee was informed that the Kerala Khadi and Village Industries Board has so far financed 2009
cooperative societies, 2161 registered institutions, 15814 individuals and 426 departmental units. The Committee was
further informed that funds allotted to the Board under Margin Money Scheme is very meagre and insufficient when
compared to the number of applications for Margin Money Assistance received in the Board. As per the guidelines of
Khadi and Village Industries Commission, the Board has to sanction the Margin Money to the beneficiaries, based on
the project report approved by the banks. Most of the projects received in the Board under Margin Money Scheme
involve huge project costs and smaller projects are almost always neglected. The Board would like to give priority to
projects involving low project cost. As per letter No. REGP/M-211/2001-2002 dated 27.12.2001, the Khadi and Village
Industries Commission has instructed the Board to give priority to smaller projects.

4.5       The State Government extends 10% rebate on retail sale of Khadi throughout the year. It purchases 75% of the

welfare of Khadi workers. The following benefits are extended to the Khadi workers by the Welfare Fund Board.
BENEFITS
            1.         Pension to khadi artisans with a minimum of Rs. 100/- and a maximum of Rs. 300/- per month on

4.7       The Committee observes that Kerala is a leading State in the welfare measures for khadi artisans. The
State Khadi Workers' Welfare Fund is a model to be examined by other States for implementation. The State
Government gives support to the Kerala Khadi and Village Industries Board by providing substantial funds
under plan fund in addition to non-plan funds for salary and rebate. A rebate of 10% on the sale of khadi is
available throughout the year. The State Government has introduced an incentive scheme to the khadi artisans
@ 10 paisa per hank in weaving. Further, the State Government has reserved a portion of Khadi materials for
the requirement of hospital to be procured from the Kerala Khadi and Village Industries Board. The Committee
appreciates and recognizes the efforts of the State Government in extending support to Khadi and Village Sector.

4.8       The Kerala Khadi and Village Industries Board is running 163 numbers of sales outlets. A considerable quantity
of Khadi and Village Industries products produced by the Board and its aided units are being sold out through these
outlets. Nowadays, Board is giving particular attention in opening more sales outlets under the direct control of the
Board. The objective behind this is to dispose of the heavy accumulation of Khadi goods turned out in the production
centres.

Officers are also running 20 of Khadi Grama Soubhagyas in all districts. There are 49 agency Bhavans and 84 numbers
of Grama Soubhagyas attached to the production units. The total sales achieved during 2001-2002 from all the Grama
Soubhagyas is Rs. 847.90 lakhs.

great demand in Kerala. The Board is also thinking of supplying the products to other State Boards. Similarly the Board

CENTRAL  SILVER  PLANT,  KUTTUR,  TRICHUR
4.14     The Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC) has set up a Central Silver Plant (Muslin Project) at
Kuttur, near Trichur for ensuring supply of silver/roving to the institutions of this State. The centre caters to the need of
silver/roving to the institutions of West Bengal, Tamil Nadu, U.P., Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra and Gujarat also. The
total supply of roving within the State comes to around 2 lakh kgs., and that of outside the State comes to 1.40 lakh kgs.
During 2001-02, the production of the unit was 3.69 lakh kgs. worth Rs. 441.00 lakhs. The actual sale was to the tune of
3.40 lakh kgs. for an amount of Rs. 419.00 lakhs. The accrued profit as on 31.3.2002 is to the extent of Rs. 176.15 lakhs.
The total investment of the plant and machinery of the unit is Rs. 166.18 lakhs. The silver/roving is being supplied to
the institutions on credit against the rebate payment so that the working capital is not blocked and ensured continued
production.
4.15     The Committee observes that Kerala being a consumer State more silver plants on the pattern of Central
Siler Plants, Kuttur, Trichur should be set up so that demands of the State of Khadi Products can be met.
BIO-TECHNOLOGY/NON-CONVENTIONAL  ENERGY  PROGRAMME
4.16     "Bio-technology and Non-conventional Energy" is one of the major industries functioning in Kerala. Various
programmes such as national project on biogas development, community/institutional and night-soil based higher
capacity biogas plants etc. are being implemented as per the guidelines and financial support of the Ministry of Non-
conventional Energy Sources. During 2001-02, 300 biogas plants, 3 Nos. of institutional and night soil based plants

            The Committee observes that in order to identify the drawbacks in the functioning of the Khadi institutions and
to take timely remedial measures, KVIC should closely monitor Khadi institutions under various categories like A, B, C
and D especially those institutions whose functioning is not at the desired level. KVIC should ensure decentralization in
decision making and delegation of more powers to State KVIB alongwith development of a strong monitoring
system.     (Para 2.4)
            The Committee observes that Khadi sales pick up only when rebate is offered to the customers. Sans rebate,
khadi sales have shown downward trend during the year. The Committee recommends that KVIC should encourage
individual entrepreneurs to sell khadi products on commission basis. There should also be attempt to make the khadi
products cheaper, qualitatively better and market competitive.      (Para 2.6)
            The Committee during the interactive session with KVIC/AP KVIB, was informed about the malpractices and
mismanagement at various levels of the Khadi institutions. The Committee is of the view that this may be one of the
reasons of cost of khadi going up and products being unaffordable. The Committee, therefore, recommends that certain
in-house activities like concurrent evaluation, data collection etc. of these institutions should be verified by outside
professional agencies.                                              (Para 2.8)
            The Committee observes that there is vast scope for implementation of the programmes like pottery (Mineral
based industry), mango jelly (fruits and vegetables processing industry), palm gur, lime industry, beekeeping, carpentry
and blacksmith, rural transport, processing of cereals and pulses, medicinal plants, paper bags conversion units, service
sector industries, dhabas and fast food units under tourism, bio-manure. Under the UNDP training programme
extraction of banana fibre programme is going to be organized by batches at Kasturba Gandhi National Memorial Trust,
Seethanagaram, Rajahmundry, East Godavari District. There is need to explore their potential in the state as these areas
have not been tapped. The Committee, therefore, recommends that efforts should be made by KVIC/KVIB to develop
these programmes in the State on priority basis and realize their fullest potential. NGOs may also be invited and
encouraged to popularize these programmes.    (Para 2.11)
            The Committee observes that cluster approaches need to be encouraged in a big way in the rural sector as it not
only builds community spirit but also provides employment at a low cost. The Committee recommends that proposals

INTRODUCTION
I, the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, having been authorised by the
Committee, hereby present this Ninety-seventh Report on the Action Taken by the Government on the recommendations contained in the
74th Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry on Demands for Grants for (2002-03) pertaining to
the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries.
2.      The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry considered and adopted the Draft report at its meeting held
on the 11th December, 2002.
3.      The 74th Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry was presented to Rajya Sabha and laid
on the Table of Lok Sabha on the 14th May, 2002.
11 December, 2002
NEW DELHI;
Dr.  P.C. ALEXANDER
Chairman,
Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry
REPORT
        The Ninety-seventh Report of the Committee deals with the Action Taken by the Government on the recommendations contained in
the 74th Report of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry on the Demands for Grants (2002-03)
pertaining to the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries which was presented to Rajya Sabha and laid on the Table of Lok Sabha on the
14th May, 2002.
2.     Action Taken Notes have been received from the Government in respect of the recommendations contained in the Report. They have
been categorized as follows:
(i)    Recommendations/Observations, which have been accepted by the Government:- Paras: 3.24, 3.27, 3.28, 3.30, 3.32, 3.35, 3.36,
3.41, 4.2, 4.3, 5.5, 5.6, 5.9, 5.11, 6.9, 6.10, 6.12, 6.13, 6.14, 6.15 (Chapter-I).
(ii)    Recommendations/Observations which the Committee does not desire to pursue in view of the Government's replies: - Paras :
1.2, 3.2, 3.37, 6.1, 6.3, 6.4, 6.5 (Chapter - II).
(iii)   Recommendations/Observations in respect of which the Committee has not accepted replies of the Government: - Paras: 3.9,
3.10, 3.12, 3.15, 6.6, 6.7, 7.5 (Chapter - III).
(iv)   Recommendations/Observations in respect of which final replies of the Government have not been received: - Paras: 3.13,
3.20, 3.21, 3.22, 3.42, 6.16, 6.17 (Chapter - IV).
(v)   Observations/Recommendations at a Glance (Chapter - V).
3.     The Committee is pleased to observe that the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries has accepted its recommendations as mentioned
in Chapter-I of the Report.
4.     In respect of the recommendations made in Chapter-II the Committee is convinced with the logic and explanation advocated by the
Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries and therefore does not want to pursue further.
5.     The Committee expresses its concern over the non-implementations of Recommendations contained in Chapter-III and therefore the
Committee desires that the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries would furnish logical explanation in respect of these recommendations.
6.     In respect of Recommendations placed in Chapter-IV, the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries has either furnished the interim
replies or couched its language in vague terms like the Ministry's views have been conveyed to concerned agencies, therefore, the
Committee desires that the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries would furnish Action Taken Note in respects of recommendations
categorized in Chapter-IV in detail and to the point, as per the intention and spirit of the recommendations of the Committee.
7.     The details of the ATR is being discussed in various Chapters in the succeeding pages.

Internal Resource Generation by KVIC
Para 3.24
        The Committee, therefore, recommends that KVIC should take steps to generate internal resources on its own so as to reduce the
dependence on budgetary resources of the Government as far as possible, by evolving suitable mechanisms like revamping of KVIC
staff, aggressive marketing of KVI products, brand building and other measures so that it becomes self-sufficient and self-reliant. A long-
term strategy for suitable positioning of Khadi for the next 5-10 years needs to be prepared, otherwise the very survival of KVIC as an
institution would be in doubt.
Comments
        The suggestions made have been noted and communicated to the KVIC for taking further necessary action.
Unspent Balance of KVIC
Para 3.27
        The Committee views with concern that KVIC had an unspent balance of Rs. 147.51 crore as on 31st March, 2001. This is not a
healthy trend, as non-utilisation of money earmarked for a specific purpose does not augur well for the premier institution. The money
should have been put to better use.
Comments
        The point suggested has been noted and communicated to the KVIC for strict compliance.
Budget Management by KVIC
Para 3.28
        The Committee recommends that in cases where lapses had been continuing over the years, responsibility should be fixed and better
budget management undertaken. This would be a major step forward. The Committee recommends further that expenditure framework
needs to be strengthened. This would involve identifying current and future financial requirements, and deviations from the prescribed
procedure should not be allowed under any circumstances.
Comments
        Suggestions made have been noted and communicated to the KVIC for strict compliance.
Non-Plan Expenditure of KVIC
Para 3.30
        The Committee finds that non-plan allocation for Khadi and Village Industries shows an increasing trend. It is also not managed
efficiently while KVIC is over-staffed. The Committee recommends that KVIC should undertake trimming exercise for reducing surplus
staff by extending VRS in order to curtail non-plan expenditure and to make the institution economically viable.
Comments:
        The suggestions made has been noted and communicated to the KVIC for further necessary action However, it may be clarified that
the expenditure under non-plan has increased to meet expenditure against salary and wages for which adequate provision did not exist
earlier. The expenditure earlier was being met through diversion of other funds/earnings.
Report of Arther Andersen on KVIC
Para 3.32
        The Committee observes that the report of Arthur Andersen was submitted in September, 2000 and is still under examination by the
KVIC. The Committee recommends that the examination of the report be expedited and a final view be taken without further delay.
Comments
        The direction has been noted.
Inventory
Paras 3.35 and 3.36

        The five year EXIM policy announced on 1st April, 2002 seeks to enable Indian artisans, Cottage and Small Industries to venture
out overseas and adopt the world as their market. The new policy makes exports free, easy and possibly rewarding. This assumes special
significance especially when India ranks low in global competition given global slowdown and domestic recession. The EXIM policy is
comprehensive, encompassing agro sector, cottage and handicrafts and small scale sectors thus taking care of more than 80% of the
population living in rural areas.
Comments
        A draft scheme for export promotion of KVI products under the EXIM policy has been formulated which has been sent for vetting to
Finance Wing. It will be implemented very shortly.

        The Committee therefore, recommends that in view of the importance of this sector, diversified forms of coir products and product
mix should be attempted. Research programmes should be undertaken by the Coir Board for improving the quality of the coir fibre, for

        The recommendations have been noted for further action. However, in this connection it is stated that under the UNDP assisted
project, the Coir Board has entered into a collaborative project with the National Institute of Design, Ahmedabad for stratetgic Design

        As recommended by the Committee, the Board is taking efforts in association with the private sector for promoting export of coir

for setting up coir pith processing units for which assistance to the tune of 25% of the capital investment on work shed and equipment

Para 5.9
        The Committee observes that coir sector employs 5 lakh people and it has the potential of expanding its activities. Although the
funds allocation for the sector has been doubled in the Ninth Five Year Plan from what it was in the Eighth Five Year Plan, (Rs. 31 crores

        The Committee appreciates the measure for welfare for the people, especially women, engaged in the coir industry which remains

        The recommendations of the Committee have been noted for future guidance.

Para 6.9
        The Committee observes that the crux of the problem lies in the recovery scenario under PMRY which has been showing a

may continue. The Chairman/Managing Directors - All India Scheduled Commercial Banks may be suitably advised by the RBI to

Achievement of Target under PMRY
Paras 6.10, 6.11, 6.12, and 6.13
6.10 The Committee futher observes that though the Government achieved in some measure quantitative target of the PMRY, no efforts
were made either by the Government or by other agencies to evaluate the qualitative achievement of the scheme. The beneficiaries
experienced difficulties in starting and running the venture. The major problem in starting the unit was in getting the loan. 50% of the

6.11 The Committee finds that shortage of funds for working capital is hindering the PMRY beneficiaries. They could not execute their

6.12 The high cost of operation is another problem where 20% of the industries were affected by this and they could not compete in the
local market. Increase in the cost of spare parts are the main cost accelerating items and entrepreneurs could not repay the interest in time.

6.13 As regards the undue delay in giving loans by banks, the Committee impresses upon banks to avoid undue delay. The Committee
recommends that implementing banks should be advised by the RBI to sanction the applications within the prescribed time frame and

there is no inordinate gap between sanction and disbursement of loan vide  their Letter No. RPCD.SP.BC.34/09.04.01/1994-45 dated

        Delay in getting power connection affected 30% of them in terms of production and marketing. Delay in getting delivery of assets

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS WHICH THE COMMITTEE DOES NOT DESIRE TO PURSUE IN VIEW OF
THE GOVERNMENT'S REPLIES
Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries
Para 1.2
        The Committee welcomes the formation of the new Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries. It has satisfied the long-felt need for the
creation of a new Ministry which would look exclusively after the needs of this sector. This is expected to give a boost to the sector,
especially when our industries now face competition from global companies and find it hard to survive.
Comments
        No comments are required.
Constitution of KVIC
Para 3.2
        The Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry in its 49th Report on Demands for Grants (2002-03)
pertaining to Ministry of Small Scale Industries and Agro and Rural Industries had expressed its concern at the inordinate delay in
reconstituting the Khadi and Village Industries Commission. The term of the previous Khadi and Village Industries Commission expired
in September, 1999 and since then the Commission had been non-existent which adversely affected the working of Khadi and Village
Industries. The Committee has been informed that the Commission has been reconstituted w.e.f. 2nd October, 2001. The Committee
welcomes the reconstitution of the Commission and hopes that the new Commission will be able to take care of the requirements of the
Khadi sector to make it self sustaining and vibrant.
Comments
        No comments are required.
Poor Quality and Design of Khadi Products
Para 3.37
        The Committee observes that poor quality and poor designs have resulted in poor sales and accumulation of large inventories. The
working cycle of production sales-cash-realization for Khadi is long and substantial funds are blocked as working capital for Khadi
institutions. This has adversely affected performance.
Comments
        The slump in Khadi performance was mainly attributed to the production of goods, which are not as per demand and taste of the
market. It was a fact that most of the Khadi producing institutions located in rural areas could not cope up with fast changing consumer
tastes particularly in cotton textile materials. This has to a large extent, resulted in the accumulation of inventory. One of the important
requirements in the above backdrop is the improvement in the quality and design of Khadi products. The Government of India is
implementing the Khadi package for Khadi and Village Industries programme which envisages better design development, quality
assurance standards etc. On implementation of such measures it is expected that the performance of Khadi sector would improve
considerably.
Employment Generation Under PMRY
Para 6.1
        The PMRY has emerged as a major Central Sector Scheme for employment generation among the educated unemployed youth, by
providing financial and other entrepreneurial development assistance in establishing self-employment ventures. Significant progress has

Wardha Institute
Para 3.9
        The Committee welcomes this move as it aught to provide a great fillip to the sector. Simultaneously, the Committee notes that there
is no specific provision in the Budget for the required funds to implement the announcement of upgrading the Wardha Institute as a
National Institute named after Mahatma Gandhi. The Committee is of the opinion that there is a need for additional provision of at least
Rs.100 crores for the Mahatma Gandhi Institute of Rural Industrialisation, Wardha. This provision may be spread over a period of three
years.
Comments
        The Khadi and Village Industries Commission, Mumbai (KVIC), a statutory body under the administrative control of the Ministry of
Agro and Rural Industries has entered into a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) and the IIT, Delhi in April, 2001 to implement a
three-year Project for revamping of the existing Jamnalal Bajaj Central Research Institute (JBCRI), Wardha and convert it into Mahatma
Gandhi Institute for Rural Industrialisation (MGIRI). The duration of the Project is 3 years (May-2001 - April-2004). The total allocation
for the project is Rs. 8.35 crores. A total of Rs. 5.70 crores has so far been released to the KVIC under S&T including funds for the
implementation of this Project and the balance will be released in due course during the project period. It is hoped that the project will be
completed during the stipulated time-frame and within the total project outlay. There has not been any project cost revision-requiring
provision of Rs.100 crores. The project implementation is constantly under review to ensure that there are no slippages in the completion
of the project.
FURTHER  RECOMMENDATION
        Since this is an important national project, the Committee feels that it should be completed by April, 2004. The Committee
impresses upon the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries to keep on vigil on the progress of the project.
R&D for KVIC
Para 3.10
        The Committee observes that R&D is the need of the hour if industries are to compete globally and growth in the sector is to be
stimulated. The Committee, therefore, recommends that allocation for Research and Development for KVIC requires be increased. If
need be, joint collaboration with foreign firms may to be taken up.
Comments
        The Ministry is alive to the significance of R&D to promote global competitiveness of the indigenous industries. Therefore,
Government in its effort to strengthen Village Industries (VIs) for production of quality marketable goods, has been making substantial
funding to help organizations and entrepreneurs to promote their existing sphere of activities. But very little investment has gone into
research and development of support services infrastructure to promote and disseminate improved technology to increase productivity
and quality standards of goods produced in rural areas by the Village Industries.
        The inputs of S&T for Technology Upgradation, transfer of appropriate technology, quality assessment of associated inputs, Quality
Control/Assurance Mechanism of final products are some of the important areas where organizations like Khadi and Village Industries
Commission (KVIC), Mumbai under this Ministry, could play an important role either through its own infrastructure or using
infrastructure available elsewhere for the strengthening of Rural Industrialisation.
        In order to provide such inputs to the Village Industries sector in the country, Government has approved the following as part of the
Khadi Package announced in May, 2001:-
A.    Strengthening of the existing S&T/R&D infrastructure of the KVIC.
B.     To establish technical inter faces with the technical establishments in the country.
C.    Networking of Quality Testing/Certifying laboratories/Institutions in the country.
        Institutions have been selected by the Government for upgrading R&D facilities. As per the package announced by the Government

97th Report of Committee on Industry
file:///D/Committee%20on%20Industry/97threport.htm[04-07-2016 12:21:53]
of India, funds allotted under sector specific R&D will be utilized to the tune of Rs. 1550 lakhs over a three years period.
        Similarly, Technical Back-up Units (TBUs/Interfaces) covering the entire country at some S&T institutes will be set up. All these
units will form a network. The proposed Mahatma Gandhi Institute for Rural Industrialisation at Wardha will be the main node of this
network.
        In order to strengthen the quality assurance labs, the KVIC will enter into MoUs with existing laboratories recognized by the
National Accredition Board for Laboratories (NABL) which will cover both the public sector as well as private sector. KVIC products
will be standard sized according to BIS/AGMARK/FPO/ etc. Adequate budget provision will be made for strengthening of the quality
control laboratories.
FURTHER  RECOMMENDATION
        The strengthening of the existing S&T/R&D infrastructure of the KVIC was announced in May, 2001 but not much progress
has been made in the matter. The Committee recommends that this project should be completed in a definite time-frame.
JPRGY
Para 3.12
        While appreciating this initiative, the Committee expresses its concern that JPRGY should not meet the fate of NPRI (National
Programme for Rural Industrialisation as announced in the Budget for the financial year 1999-2000. The allocation of Rs.40 lakhs was
kept for the NPRI scheme in the BE 2001-02 which was reduced to nominal amount of Rs.1.00 lakh in the RE of that year. The scheme is
yet to take off. However, in the BE  2002-03 a provision of Rs. 90 lakhs has been made. The Committee, therefore impresses upon the
Ministry to review the progress of NPRI so that the earlier mistakes are not repeated by the administration.
Comments
        The scheme on NPRI was announced in the year 1999-2000 with a mission to set up 100 rural clusters every year. Office of the DC
(SSI) was made the coordinating agency of the programme. KVIC, SIDBI and NABARD are the major implementing agencies. No fund
was provided separately for the programme and it was felt that various Ministries/Departments were having their own programmes in this
area which could be coordinated and their synergies exploited for better impact.
        Efforts were made to firm up the scheme at the initial stage. A number of meetings were called in which all the agencies involved in
rural industrialization participated. A national level Steering Committee was constituted under the Chairmanship of Secretary (SSI &
ARI) to guide, implement and monitor the programme. Consequently, KVIC identified 50 clusters for development for each year, SIDBI
25 and NABARD 50 for a period of 5 years. So far, KVIC has launched the programme in 20 clusters, NABARD in 14 and SIDBI in 13.
The other clusters are also under consideration and preliminary/diagnostic studies are being conducted of these clusters. It was, however,
felt that some fund was required for certain gap filling exercises towards cluster intervention. Therefore, the Office of the DC (SSI)
launched a scheme on NPRI in the year 2001-02 to supplement the efforts of the various agencies. The amount provided in the scheme is
only Rs.5 lakhs per cluster. The purpose of financial assistance is to fill certain gaps in the development of clusters, and it does not
constitute the entire amount required for such development. As the scheme has been approved in the year 2001-02, it is expected to yield
results in the coming years.
FURTHER  RECOMMENDATION
        The Committee fails to understand as to why a scheme is announced by the Government without any budgetary provision. Ministry's
reply that no fund was provided separately for the programme and it was felt that various Ministries/Departments were having their own
programmes in this area which could be coordinated and their synergy exploited for their impact does not appear to be sound because this
Committee has its own experience that coordination among Central Ministries and Departments is a difficult preposition to achieve. The
Committee now expects that with the provision of funds the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries would implement the programme.

Para 3.15

sector, it is necessary to provide and offer products that match consumer preferences.
Comments

FURTHER  RECOMMENDATION

regard.

Recommendations    (Para 7.1.7)
 
MODERNISATION OF THE GEOLOGICAL SURVEY OF INDIA
The Committee understands that in the wake of radical reforms in economic and mineral policies of the country, up-to-
date high quality database for optimum development of natural resources both on land and offshore, management of
natural hazards and protection of environment became essential. A quantum jump to the modernisation and technology
up gradation in all spheres of activity is prerequisite for the goal.
Action Taken
            The Department is giving full support to the modernization efforts and capacity building of GSI so that GSI is
geared to make available the high quality database for optimum development of natural resources both onland and off
shore.
 
Recommendations  (Para 7.1.8 )
EARTHQUAKE STUDIES BY THE GEOLOGICAL SURVEY OF INDIA       
After the devastating effect of the Gujarat earthquake, the Committee feels more emphasis should be given on the
earthquake studies to save human lives and property in the urban as well rural areas. The Committee recommends the
adequates funds may be made available to the G.S.I. for the purpose. The G.S.I. should also take the aid and assistance
of the experts available across the World.
Action Taken
GSI has given thrust to active fault mapping and microzonation studies of urban clusters, as a part of earthquake
studies towards deleneation of potential risk zones and mitigation of impact of disasters.  It is also collaborating with
Indian Metrological Department and participating in a Department of Science & Technology sponsored Indo-Italian
Collaborative Research Project for seismic studies.  Provision has been made for the procurement of the state-of-art
field location cum data collection equipments as a part of modernization programmes of Geological Survey of India .

Recommendations (Para 13.2)
Non-Plan Loan to Mines PSUs
The Committee   is of the opinion that   non-plan loan is a necessary evil as it is   essential   for loss making PSUs to
maintain its  operation and   separation of surplus  work force and  sometimes even to meet the  cash loss, all depending 
upon the quantum of  loss being incurred by a  PSU.  Non-plan loan is an evil in the sense   that the amount of non-plan
loan gets added to the liability of the Company, which is always a burden on the Company.  The Committee notes that
during  2002-03  no non-plan loan has been allocated to mines PSUs, although rationalisation of manpower is being 
undertaken in almost  all mines PSUs.
Action Taken
            During the year 2002-03, no non-plan loan has been allocated to the PSUs under the Department of Mines.  The
position of non-plan loan given earlier to the PSUs is as follows:
(a)
                Hindustan Copper Ltd.
(i)                  A total non-plan loan of Rs.440 crores has been converted as grant.
(ii)                Additional grant of Rs. 130 crores for rationalization of manpower is being provided.
(b)               Mineral Exploration Corporation Ltd.
(i)         The conversion of non-plan loan will be taken into account at the time of disinvestment.
 
Recommendations   (Para 13.4.5 & 13.4.6.)
FINANCIAL RESTRUCTURING OF HINDUSTAN COPPER LTD.    
The Committee is pleased to note that as a result of implementation of VRS in HCL during last three years the wage
cost as percentage of turnover has come down   from 35.81% in 1999 -2000 to 22.98% in 2000-01 and turnover per
employee has increased from Rs. 3.30 lakh to Rs.5.11 lakh during the same period.
The Committee understands that HCL is sailing through adverse financial situation and is a loss making PSU, therefore,
the Committee is in agreement with the Department of Mines regarding incapacity of repayment of non-plan loan by
HCL. The Committee   feels that since the financial restructuring     of HCL is on the card the Department of Mines
should not delay any longer the submission of the proposal for conversion of non-plan loan   of Rs.440 crore   into grant
and the Government should not hesitate in clearing the proposal, as cleaner the balance sheet   of the Company larger
the possibility of a potential purchasers coming forward.

conversion of non-plan loan of Rs.440 crores into grant. Besides following measures have also been taken:-
(i)
                  Conversion of outstanding plan loan as on March 31, 2002, amounting to Rs.71.50 crore into equity to
improve the net worth of the Company.
(ii)                Waiver of outstanding interest on plan loan amounting to Rs.25.72 crore as on March 31, 2002.
(iii)               Extension of period of the Government guarantees already provided for raising working capital term loan
by a further 2 years or disinvestments which is earlier, in order to facilitate meeting the obligations for the
Secured Bond repayment.

Recommendations Para (18.3):
Contribution Of Mining Sector To The Nation  
The Committee further observes  that the more and more private  sector players   are coming to the mining sector and
mines PSUs are either have already been disinvested  i.e. BALCO  and HZL     or  are on the verge of disinvestment  as
in the  case of HCL  and NALCO and   due  to  on-going  liberalisation  process , the contribution of   mining sector  to
national exchequer would improve in the years to come.  The Committee hopes that the on-going  liberalisation process
should enhance the capabilities  of making  contribution of mining sector to the nation   and society in general.  In this
regard the  Committee  hopes that the Government would give due consideration towards  the contribution  made by
units of private  sector and PSUs in mining sector.
Action Taken
            Under the National Mineral Policy, 1993, 13 minerals hitherto reserved for exploitation by Public Sector were
thrown open for exploitation by Private Sector also and thereby provided a level playing field to private companies in
the mineral sector.  Thus entire mining sector is open for private investment including Foreign Direct
Investments(FDI).  A number of leading global mining companies have evinced interest in Indian mining sector
resulting in expected FDI inflow of Rs.3963 crores.  The National Mineral Policy, 1993 has also recognized the need for
encouraging private investment including FDI and state of art technology in the mineral sector and has therefore
contributed towards national exchequer and society in general.  Besides this, a number of amendments have been carried
out in the MMDR Act, 1957, MCR, 1960 and MCDR, 1988,  since 1994 to make Indian mining sector investor friendly
and hassle free.

Action Taken:
 
The National Mineral Policy, 1993, recognised the need for encouraging private investment including foreign
direct investment and state-of-the-art technology in mineral sector. Further , National Mineral Policy 1993 has  stressed 
that the Central  Government in consultation with the State Governments, shall continue to formulate the legal measures
for the regulation of mines and the development of mineral resources to ensure basic  uniformity  in mineral 
administration and to ensure that the development of mineral resources keeps pace, and is in consonance with the
national policy goals.
 
It is therefore evident that review of the policy and consequent amendment(s) in the Mines and Minerals
(Development and Regulation) Act, 1957 and rules framed there under to cater to future demands is(are)  an ongoing
process, and can not be a one time exercise.
 
 For a structured  and institutionalized review of the policies and procedures affecting the mining and the mineral
sector and for all matters connected or incidental thereto, the Mineral Advisory Council has been constituted by the
Government. The Hon’ble Minister for Coal and Mines is the Chairman of the Council. The Council has balanced
representation from State Governments, Industry Associations , Experts in mining sector as well as Members of
Parliament. The Mineral Advisory Council inter alia reviews the status of implementation of the National Mineral
Policy, advises the Government on mineral policy and legislation and the status of the mining and the mineral sector,
including inter alia  all the issues identified by the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry in its Report.
 
After the National Mineral Policy was announced, Mines and Minerals (Development and Regulation) Act, 1957
has been amended in 1994 and 1999. After amendment in the Principal Act in 1999, the Mineral Concession Rules,
1960 have been amended on January 17,.2000, September 25,.2000,January 22,2000, and on January 11.,2002 .
Similarly, after 1999, the Mineral Conservation and Development Rules 1988 have been amended on 17.1.2000,
25.9.2000 and 11.1.2002.
The  amendments in the legislation have been extensively discussed prior to their enactment and honed as per
recommendations of the Mineral Advisory Council in its various meetings. As a recent example, minerals for which the
State Governments would be empowered to approve mining plans have been identified, time limits have been prescribed
for  conveying a decision on application(s) for mineral concessions and mining plans, and fees payable for various
applications under the rules have been revised as per recommendations of the Mineral Advisory Council.
 
            Two meetings of the Mineral Advisory Council have been held since 1999. In addition the Department of Mines
organized a Conference of State Ministers of Mining and Geology, as well as a Tripartite Meeting of the Central
Government, State Governments and Investors in the Mining Sector in 2001. These meetings also discussed inter alia
the issues identified by the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry. The review of the National Mineral Policy
and the other issues identified by the Parliamentary Standing Committee will therefore appropriately be listed for
discussion in the next meeting of the Mineral Advisory Committee.         
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
            The Committee expects  that the  Department of Mines  understands the concern  of Department related
Parliamentary  Standing Committee on Industry  and  therefore  appreciate its desire accordingly.  Interchanging and
intermingling  and  the functions of  Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee with  Mineral Advisory
Council  would not only be belittling and undermining the status of  this Committee   but also juxtaposing  the role   of
Mineral Advisory Council.    The Department of Mines placed  the issues identified  by the Parliamentary Standing
Committee on Industry in the meetings of  Mineral Advisory Council  but deprived the Committee of the outcome of the
meetings and  discussion held.  The Committee recommends that the Department of Mines should  furnish the details of 
Action Taken in its Note and  apprise the Committee comprehensively.   The Committee recommends that  the
Department of Mines should forward the  minutes of the meeting of Mineral Advisory  Council  to this Committee
whenever  the Mineral Advisory Council discusses the issues identified by the Committee.

FOREIGN INVESTMENT IN MINING SECTOR
 The Committee appreciates  the  efforts made by the Department of Mines towards making the  mining sector more  
investor friendly  but  at the same time hopes that  pace of foreign  investment  in the mining sector may be  
accelerated.
Action Taken:
            The liberalisation of policy has provided a conducive atmosphere for the international mining companies to
invest in the country and bring with this investment and world class mining technology.  The policy of the Government
of India has been to actively encourage foreign investors to participate in the exploration and production of minerals and
mineral based industries.  Sustained inflow of private including foreign investment is desirable to bring in state-of-the-
art technology, coupled with foreign capital for the exploration and exploitation of mineral resources and in-country
value addition.
            As a part of the policy to actively encourage such investments, in order to give a further push for the FIPB
approved projects to get off the ground quickly, a monitoring system has been put in place.  This involves a periodic
review by the Foreign Investment Implementation Authority (FIIA), which looks at the progress made in implementing
the major projects.  Also, within each Ministry, there is a Fast Tract Committee (FTC) which closely monitors the
projects in that particular sector.
            The Department of Mines has been effectively utilizing various international fora, to highlight the policy and
legislative initiatives undertaken to project India as an attractive investment destination and the opportunities available. 
In this context the response has been good.
            Meetings with foreign investors have also been organized to identify the problems in implementation of various
Projects.  A time frame for disposal of applications for mineral concessions have also been fixed in the Mineral
Concession Rules.  These initiatives will accelerate the inflow of foreign investment in the mining sector.
FURTHER RECOMMENDATION
            The Committee observes that the Department of Mines have  furnished in its Action Taken Note only the
institutional  arrangement for accelerating  the pace  of foreign investment in the Mining Sector   but that is not
sufficient, the Committee feels.  The  Department of Mines should have furnished the details of  course of action
undertaken to promote foreign investment in the mining sector, region and  mineral-wise  and the outcome of efforts  so
made in the  form of quantum of  foreign investment.  The Committee recommends that FIIA and FTC should play  pro-
active role   for promotion of foreign investment.

MEETING SOCIAL OBLIGATION AND DISCHARGING SOCIAL RESPONSIBILITIES AND DUTIES

and duties.   These units in the mining sector should contribute towards development.   The   Committee hopes that
regulation and development of mineral resources would be carried on in such a manner that, the mining sector is on the
course of sustainable development.  
Action Taken
Mining contributes tremendously to the socio economic development of the people in the backward and tribal
areas of the country by upgrading infrastructure and other amenities and opening them to the mainstream of national
development.  However, this fact is not fully realized in many quarters. There is a  need felt  need to bring together
mining industry, Government. officials and NGOs and other interested groups to discuss socio economic development
of the people in these areas through mining activities.  In this background, a Conference was recently organized by
Federation of Indian Mineral Industries (FIMI) on 31
st Jan. and 1 st Feb.2002 in Jaisalmer, Rajasthan to sensitise the
Industry and  State Governments on social and community issues.
A number of amendments have been carried out in the Mines and Minerals (Development & Regulation) Act,
1957 in 1994 and 1999 and corresponding amendments in Mineral Concession Rules, 1960 and Mineral Conservation
and Development Rule, 1988 have also been made to make mining sector investor friendly and hassle free.  A number

FIRST REPORT OF THE COMMITTEE 
I, the Chairman, Department Related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry, 
having been authorised by the Committee to present the Report on its behalf, present this 
First Report of the Committee on the Demands for Grants for 1993-94 of the Ministry of 
Industry. 
2. In pursuance of Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the Rajya Sabha 
pertaining to Department Related Standing Committees, Hon-'ble Chairman, Rajya Sabha 
and Hon 'ble Speaker, Lok Sabha nominated 42 members of Rajya Sabha and Lok Sabha to 
the Committee on Industry for the functions assigned to it under the Rules. Further 
Chairman, Rajya Sabha and Speaker, Lok Sabha decided that all the provisions of Rule 270 
of the Rules relating to the functions of the Committee shall become operative with effer1 
from 30th March, 1993. 
3. The Committee on Industry deals with the subjects falling in the jurisdiction of t11e 
Ministry of Industry, Ministry of Steel and Ministry of Mines. 
4. The Committee accordingly held its first meeting on the 22nd April, 1993 and 
considered relevant documents and papers received from the Ministry of Industry, on the 
Demands for Grants for the year 1993-94. 
5. The Committee also heard the oral evidence of the Secretaries of the various 
Department s of the Ministry of Industry on the performance budget in the context of 
Demands for Grants of the Ministry of Industry.

considered and adopted the Report at its sitting held on 4th May, 1993.
