8.0       STRENGTHS, WEAKNESSES,  OPPORTUNITIES AN D THREADS (SWOT)
ANALYSIS OF PMRY. 
Strengths: 
                  1.            The spread of the Scheme is uni form in both urban as well as  rural areas of the country. As
per the findings of the second round of the evaluation on the PMRY disbursement of the
beneficiaries in rural and urban areas is 49.9% and 50.1% respectively. 
                  2.            Against the target of 18 lakh, loans have been  sanctioned to 20.40 lakh and disbursed to 
16.00 lakh educated unempl oyed youth between 1993-94 – 2001-02.  Employment 
opportunities have been  estimated to be created for about 24 lakh people during the same
period. 
                  3.            According to 2nd round of Evaluation study, assets that have been created is 89.7% of cases 
disbursed loan. 
Weaknesses: 
Declining recovery rate: 
                  1.            The recovery of loan overdue s under the PMRY Scheme has been declining.  It was 37.2
per cent for the half year ending March 2000 and has come down to 34.8 per cent for the half
year ending March 2002.   
                  2.            The overall amount of loan di sbursed under the Scheme has been stagnating around Rs.57,
000/- to Rs.58, 000/- per beneficiar y despite enhancement in th e maximum project cost from
Rs.1 lakh to Rs.2 lakh. 
                  3.            There is gap between number of cases sanctioned and disbursed by banks.

                  4.            During VIII plan, the disbursement was 6.52 lakh against sanction of 7.75 lakh.  Similarly,
for the IX plan disbursement was 9.48 lakh against the sanction of 12.66 lakhs. 
Opportunities: 
                  1.            In a situation where employme nt opportunities in organized sectors and Govt. sectors have
been virtually stagnating or declining, PMRY Scheme has emerged a major scheme o f
employment generation in the country. 
                  2.            The successful self employed units set up under the PMRY can graduate into higher scale 
units creating further consequent employment for other unemployed persons. 
                  3.            The cost of employment generation is about Rs.5000/- per person to the Central Exchequer.
Threats: 
The bank/financial institutions can help successful  PMRY units to graduate successfully into
higher scale of operation.   
8.1       The Committee recommends that the Mini stry of ARI should make in -depth SWOT analysis o f 
PMRY and thereafter undertakes massive action for combating its thr eats, and overcoming its
weaknesses.  More and more avenues should be explored for tracing oppor tunities for employment
generation.  The Committee is of the view that the best cr iteria to assess the opera tional efficiency of a
programme are to observe its spread and its capaci ty to serve the down- tr odden people and its welfare 
instinct and its inherent strength to  uplift the standard of living of pe ople in general.  Adequate measure
may be undertaken fo r popularization of PMRY a nd for changing the mind set of financial institutions
for making it pro customer and with further enhanced budgetary allocation, PMRY could make a dent in
the india’s year of problems of  unemployment and poverty.  PMRY division may also undertake cost 
benefit analysis of the pr ogramme and effort should be made for ensuring that actions are being taken
for achieving the basic objectives of the programme in a time bound frame.

9.8       As per the norms of sponsoring laid down by the Govt. of India, applic ations to be sponsored to
banks are 125% of the target.  Hence, it is likely that after each of the financial year, there are some
pending applications with the impl ementing agencies.  As per the in structions issued by the Govt. o f
India and RBI, the eligible pending applications are to be considered in the next financial year. 
9.9       As per the reports received from the RBI, 93,659 applications were  pending with banks as on
30.11.02. For minimizing the rejection of  applications by banks, the RB I has informed that they have
requested banks to carry out a sample check of rejected application to ascertain the reasons fo r
rejections.  The review of the reje cted applications is to be carried  out at a level higher than the one
rejecting the applications. For avoiding stoppage/delay of disbursements, the RBI has initiated following
steps: 
                  1.            Banks have been instructed to dispose off the applications for loans upto Rs.25, 000 within
2 weeks and for loans above Rs.25, 000/- within 8-9 weeks.   
                  2.            Banks have been instructed to adhere to the quarterly schedule for sanction an d
disbursement of loans to avoid unnecessarily delays under the Scheme.   
                  3.            It has been decided that if ‘no dues certificate’ from other banks  in the area is not received 
within 15 days of request for ve rification then it will be presumed that the applicants is not
having any dues from the other banks. 
c)      State/UTs have been requested to  instruct DICs to dispose of f the applications within one 
month of the receipt of applic ations. Banks have been author ized to receive applications
directly under the Scheme. 
9.10     Following steps have been initiated for ensuring coverage of SC/STs as per the norms: 
                  1.            While communicating the annual target to State/UTs and ba nks, they are requested to 
ensure 22.5% coverage for SC/STs under the PMRY. 
                  2.            Maximum eligible age limit has been re laxed from 18-35 year s to 18-45 years fo r 
applicants from SC/ST categories. 
                  3.            Part of the funds released for contingency to State/UTs can be ut ilised for motivational 
purposes with emphasis on SC/ST, Women and Minorities. 
9.11     The Plan targets under the Scheme are communicated to State/UTs & the RBI before the start of
the next financial year in the first week of the following financial year. The State/UTs have been advised
to constitute Task Force at Block Level/Mandal Level.  The states have  been permitted to utilize part o f
the funds released for contingency for motivationa l/familiarization programmes purposes with emphasis
on SC/STs, Women and Minorities etc. 
9.12     The original guidelines of the PMRY Scheme provide that not more than 30% enterprises should
be from business sector.  However, the modifi ed guidelines under impl ementation since 1.4.99 do not
provide for any minimum stipulat ion of projects under industry s ector or maximum stipulation o f
projects under business sector.  It wa s found that despite enhancement in  project cost fr om Rs.1 lakh to
Rs.2 lakh, the average loaning under the Scheme  has been stagnating around Rs.60,000 per beneficiary
rendering it difficult to set up an y industrial activity out of this.  In addition, settin g up of projects under

industry sector requires getting power connections, licence and NOCs etc.  Hence, few people are opting
for projects under industry sector.  The average employment generation per unit set up under the PMRY
is 1.5 per disbursed loan which can come either from service and, busin ess or industry sectors.  During
the review meetings of the PMRY , it was deliberated that one of the reasons for rejection o f
applications/non disbursement of loan was the tendency to adhere  the minimum loaning from the
industry sector.  Hence, Govt. decided to waive off the max imum stipulation laid down from the
business sector.  
9.13     The Committee is of the view that the PMRY has emerged as a major Central Sector Scheme for
employment generation among the educated un employed youth, by providi ng financial and othe r
entrepreneurial development assistance in establis hing self-employment ventur es. Significant progress 
has been achieved in the implemendation of th e scheme. The Committee recommends that government
should take following steps for the success of PMRY:  
(a)    Minimise the rejection ratio by banks against no. of application received. 
(b)   Avoid the stoppage/delay of disbursement in PMRY loans on flimsy grounds. 
(c)    Quick disposal of application on the part of DICs and forwarding the same to banks. 
(d)   Coverage of SC/STs under the scheme as per the norms stipulated by Government of India. 
(e)    Timely communication of targets to banks for necessary action on their part. 
(f)     Effective orientation programmes conducted by DI C for the target groups at Block/Taluka 
level to enlighten/popularization of PMRY. 
(g)    Accordance to the provision of PMRY for advancing loans in  the ratio of 50%, 30% and 
20% in respect of industry, service and business sector. 
 9.14    The States/UTs should be advised to c onsider sponsoring more a nd more applications unde r
industry sector to ensure creation of more employment opportunities under the PMRY.   
 9.15    Evaluation and objective Assessment of PMRY 
Replying to the committee’s query  as to  the states where PMRY was a full all success; the 
states where PMRY did marginally good and the st ates where PMRY failed miserably, along with
reasons for such performance, the Ministry of Agro and Rural I ndustries stated the States where PMRY
was a full all success are Punjab and Himachal Pradesh (disburseme nt vis-à-vis targets is 80% an d 
above).  The States where PMRY is working satisfactorily are Haryana, Rajasthan, M.P. U.P.,
Maharashtra, Karnataka, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Pondicherry, Lakshadweep etc. (i.e. disbursement vis-à-
vis targets is 60% & above).  The States where PMRY has failed ar e: Delhi, J&K, West Bengal and
North Eastern States e.g. Manipur , Meghalaya, Nagaland, Tripura and Arunachal Pradesh etc. (i.e.
disbursement vis-à-vis targets ar e 30 pr cent or less). The States where disbursement under the Scheme
is 80% and above those States wh ere recovery of loan overdues is  around 55%. (Punjab – 57.3 per cent 
for the half year ended March 2001) . The States where the Scheme has been implemented satisfactorily
are the States where th e recovery of loan overdues is between 40 per cent to 45 per cent.  (i.e. Haryana
43.1 per cent; U.P. 45.6 percent; Rajasthan 42.1 per cent; Gujarat 61.2 per cent; Karnataka 48.1 per cent
for the half year ended March 2001).  The States where disbursements are less than 30% of the target are
the States where recovery of loan overdues is very low.  The recovery of lo an overdues for the period
ending March, 2001 was 1.0 per cent in Manipur 1.7 per cent in Nagaland; 13.0 per cent in Assam; 16.7
per cent in West Ben gal for the half year ended March, 2001.  In  J&K, the recovery of loan overdues is

19.16   The Committee is of the opinion that government should study the basic reasons for failure o f
PMRY in Delhi, J& K, West Bengal and North-Eastern States and specific programme should be
chalked out for making PMRY  all success in these states.  What can be more glaring than to observe
PMRY failing in Delhi, the pow erseat of governance, and it l ooks more unfortunate because a

place from where Prime Minister, as the helm of all affairs, directs the governance throughout the
country.  It casts a deep aspers ion.  The sooner the corrective meas ures are undertaken the better it
would be for casting aside aspersion on the working efficiency of governance.  
19.17   The Committee hopes that the implementati on of the recommendations of High Powered
Committee on PMRY would result in effective and smooth working of PMRY. The Committee furthe r

problems of unemployment and poverty.

11.28   Marketing Strategy of KVIC 
The marketing strategy of KVIC is to focus on its eco friendly and natural product range. Khadi
& Village Industries sector produces  goods and services both. In villa ge industries service based units
basically cover local area needs and marketing is not much of a problem. With rega rd to non-consumer 
goods normally units established have good market as most of such products are intermediary products
used by other industries. Main di fficulty is in consumer goods a nd khadi. For both these products areas
of intervention involves a detail ed marketing strategy for publicit y, branding and brand promotion,
design input, better packaging etc.  Accessing private marketing cha nnel, modernization of existing
channels, organizing large scale e xhibitions are important aspects. Marketing federations have been
formed with various village industries federations to  act as facilitator outsi de the governmental set up.
Design / packaging development scheme and renovation of marketing outlets scheme has been launched.

Cereals, Spices Powder, Pulses, Ja ggery, etc. and the same have been  launched at Mumbai and Delhi in
select Outlets.  Based on the experience it is felt that a professional Marketing Agency / Federation is
required, so that KVIC does not get involved in Departmental Trading Ac tivities, since institutions and

11.43   IMPACT OF VAT ON VILLAGE INDUSTRY PRODUCTS 
Reacting to the Committee’s que ry regarding impact of VAT on the village industry products 
Chief Executive Officer, Khadi and Village Commission commented as under:- 
“VAT has replaced the Sales Tax with effect from 01.04.2003; three St ates have already agreed to
implement it.  Most of the States had exempted us from paying Sales Tax.  Unfortunately, in the last two
to three years, Sales Tax has been imposed in cer tain States.  For exampl e, in respect of Khadi
industries, Tamil Nadu has declared rebate only fo r products produced in their States, not for those
which are coming from outside.  Si milarly, some other States have extended a rebate for only those
village industries, which are situated in their States.  In my opinion, zero- based budgeting must be done 
for the village industries sector.  We  have written to all the State Go vernments, to the chief Ministers
and the concerned ministers.  Th e Secretary has also written to the empowered committee on VAT, to
consider this viewpoint.  Also, th e minister has written a letter requesting for ‘across the board’ set-up 
for the khadi and village industries sector.  The ec onomic scale of the vill age and khadi industries is
low.  If this minor advantage of not having to pay Sales Tax is extended, it wi ll help these industries a
lot.” 
11.44   The Committee observes that 16 more states have agreed to  the VAT structure of taxation
system. However, the Committee re commends that the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries should
examine the case of feasibi lity of applying the  Zero- based budgeting for the vill age industry sector and
accordingly advocate the exemptions of tax across  the board for institution or entrepreneur, which is
registered with the Khadi and Village Industries Board or Khadi and Village Industries Commission.

12.33   COOPERATIVISATION SCHEME 
12.33.1            The objectives of the co-operati visation scheme were forma tion of viable coir co-
operatives and revitalisation of the potentially viable dormant societies and bringing the coir workers in
to the co-operative fold so that the quality a nd quantity of production impr oves, workers get bette r
wages and they are freed from e xploitation of middlemen and the i ndustry is put on a sound footing.  It
was aimed to bring 80% of the work-force in the industry under co-operative  fold through of the 
scheme. Coir Board is the m onitoring agency of the Scheme.             The objectives of the scheme are
yet to be achieved due to a mult iplicity of reasons. The Institut e of Rural Management which had
conducted an evaluative study on th e scheme, opined that the “Schem e of Co-operativisation in Coi r 
Industry as it is envisaged and implemented need s to undergo drastic revision to meet the emerging
challenges. The Integrated Coir Development Project is one of the components of the Co-operativisation 
Scheme.  It envisages setting up of new primary co-operatives, modernisation and expansion of existing 
co-operatives, improved handlooms, curling units and automatic spinni ng units etc.   The Project is 
being implemented with the assistance of National Co-operative Development Corporation (NCDC) and 
the coir producing States concerned. Assistance under this component is still being released.   
12.33.2            The Committee is of view that  the objectives of the co- operativisation scheme i.e. 
formation of viable coir co-operatives and revitalizat ion of the potentially viab le dormant societies and 
bringing the coir workers in to the co-operati ve fold  for improving th e quality and quantity o f 
production and putting industry on a sound footing is a unique mission in Coir Industry.    Therefore, the
suggestion of the Institute of Rural Management  that the Scheme of Co-operativisation in Coir Industry 
as it is envisaged and implemen ted needs to undergo drastic revisi on to meet the emerging challenges,
needs attention of the government . The National Co-operative Deve lopment Corporation (NCDC) may 
be entrusted with greater role for implementation of co-operativisation scheme. 
12.34   Model Coir Village Scheme  
12.34.1            Coir Board has been implement ing the Model Coir Village Scheme from the year 1983
which provides assistance to coir workers to improve their working and living conditions.  The
assistance is provided to coir wo rkers in all coir producing States/U Ts of the country.  During the last
three years, no villages were a dopted under the Scheme as the Mini stry did not accord sanction fo r
continuation of the scheme afte r 1999-2000.  In 1999, the Mi nistry entrusted the Institute of Rural
Management, Anand, Gujarat to conduct an evalua tive study on the implemen tation of the scheme. 
After conducting the study, the IRMA recommended that  the programme merits continuance because it
is the only one of its kind.  But it needs to be rest ructured.  In line with the recommendations of the
IRMA, the Board drafted and submitted a scheme na med Production Oriented Welfare Scheme for Coi r
Workers to the Ministry for approval. 
12.34.2            The Committee is of the view that the Ministry of ARI should approve the Production
Oriented Welfare Schemes for Coir Workers as the follow up programme of Model Coir Village Yojana
which was a unique Yojana.  After all the fruits of development must reach to the lowest rung of society
and of course the workers as well who are the actual warriors of industrialization process.  So long, India
remains a Welfare State,  the provisions for Welfa re measures must continue for carrying out the
constitutional obligations.   The Co mmittee agrees with the views of  Institute of Rural Management,
Anand, Gujarat for continuance of Model Coir Village Yojana.

12.37   Merger of Coconut Developm ent Board and Coir Board for bette r co-ordination and Integrated 
planning. 
12.37.1            Responding to the proposal of the merger of Coconut Development Board and Coi r
Board for better co-ordination a nd integrated planning, the Minist ry of ARI has communicated the
committee that the Coconut Development Board is concentrated on production of coconut while the
Coir Board is concentrated on coir fibre and allied products.  The raw- material for coir  industry is the 
coconut husk, a byproduct of coconut industry.  The focu s of the above Boards ar e different.  The coi r
industry by and large provides employment to 5,86,000 peopl e and it is an export oriented industry and
earn foreign exchange to the tune  of Rs.320 crores annually. The base of raw-material availability is 
expanded.  Technical know-how for coir industry is  lacking in the non-traditional coconut growing 
areas.  It is necessary to pr ovide the requisite technical guida nce through a professional body like Coi r
Board.   
12.37.2            The Coir Board as a separate commodity Board  could do only so much focusing
employment generation in rural areas, development of new pr oducts, skill development in non-
traditional areas, transfer of technology, etc. The me rger of Coir Board with Coconut Development
Board will lose its focus for ex clusive development of coir indus try and its positive results being
achieved. There are different types of natural fibres like bana na fibre, pineapple fibr e, sisal, bimal, etc.
available in various parts of the country.  No concerted effort has been made for the industrial use of  the
above natural fibres available in a bundance.  It is desirable to pursue   formation of a Hard Fibre Board
rather than clubbing the activitie s of Coir Board with the Coconut  Development Board.  This will
increase the employment opportunity in rural areas in all States including North-Eastern region.

15.1     The Finance Minister  in his budget speech of the year 1999-2000 announced a scheme called the 
National Programme on Rural Industr ialisation.  The purpose of the scheme is to set up 100 rural
industrial clusters in the country  every year so that it can boost up the rural economy by creating more
employment  avenues for the rural youth in the non -farm sector, and slow dow n the migration of the 
rural artisans to towns/cities. Th e 0ffice of the Developm ent Commissioner(Small Scale Industries) was
made the coordinating agency and the KVIC was envisage d to play an important role in setting up these
clusters as well as making good use of its extensive marketing outlets.  No fund was provided separately
for the programme and it was fe lt that various Ministries/ De partments are having their own
programmes in this area which could be coordi nated and their synergie s exploited for greate r
impact.Consequent upon the bifurcatio n of business between the Ministry  of SSI and Ministry of ARI,
the scheme is being coordinated by the Ministry  of ARI recently, sinc e Sep 2002. The programme is
being implemented by NABARD and SIDBI in 31 and 14 clusters respectively. So far KVIC has already
launched the programme in 22 clusters  The state wi se position of implementation  of the programme is
placed at annexure. 
15.2     In order to facilitate implementation of the programme, a scheme on NPRI ha s been formulated
which has a provision of extendi ng financial assistance of Rs. 5.0 lakhs per cluster. The budget
provision of Rs. 90 lakhs under the sche me  was reduced to      Rs. 63 lakhs at RE stage for 2002-03 as 
the proposals were not received from  the states/ UTs  and the quart erly expenditure was not made. 
During this year, i.e.  2002-03, 16 diagnostic study  proposals from 9 States/ UTs of Assam, Andaman &
Nicobar, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Kerala, Maharashtra, Orissa,  Tamil Nadu, and UP have been
approved at a cost of Rs. 8 lakhs  under the scheme on NPRI formulat ed by the Govt. of India. Funds
amounting to Rs. 8 lakhs  shall be  released after receiving requisi te information from them. The
proposals from other States/ UTs have  also been invited for financial assistance under the scheme. The
scheme on NPRI of the Ministry is basically formulated as a gap filling arra ngement. The majo r
implementing agencies of the programme are KVIC, SIDBI and NABARD.  
  
15.3     The NPRI is basically fo rmulated  to facilitate the fill ing up of crucial gaps and develop
infrastructural linkages  as an add on to schemes already being executed by  the implementing agencies,
i.e. KVIC, SIDBI , NABARD  and States. The former three agen cies are implementing this programme
from their own resources. However,  the financial support to states as  also to these agencies shall be
provided to the extent admissible. Th e Committee observes that National Pro gramme for Rural

19.0     Tiny and Micro Enterprises 
19.1     Tiny Enterprises are such units which ha ve investment in plan t and machinery upto Rs.25.00
Lakhs.   As such all such industria l activities which are el igible for registration as  SSI are also eligible
for registration in the tiny sector as  long as its investment in plant and machinery is upto the prescribed
limit of Rs.25.00 lakhs   The majori ty activities in Khadi & Coir I ndustry which are predominantly in
rural areas and have investment below Rs. 25 lakhs are covered under Tiny/Micro enterprises in Agro &
Rural Industries.  
19.2     The promotion and developm ent of the tiny sector has been a conscious policy of Government. 
A separate policy for the tiny se ctor was announced as part of the policy measures announced fo r
promotion of small, tiny and vill age industries in August, 1991.  Th e policy envisages preferential
allocation of land, power, facilities for skill/technological up- gradation, easier access to finance, priority 
in Government purchase programme and relaxation from certain labour laws, etc.   
             
19.3     To further strengthen the sector a separate policy package fo r tiny sector was announced by the 
Prime Minister as part of the Comp rehensive Policy Package for SSI on 30 th August, 2000, which 
Page 67 of 101PARLIAMENT OF INDIA

envisages separate policy support, credit support, infrastructure support an d technology and marketing
support to the Sector.  As a follow up measure, 50% of plots under IID Scheme have been earmarked for
the tiny sector.  20% of the annual projected tur nover would qualify for the purpose of working capital
loans, concessional rate of interest from NSIC  on composite loans up to Rs.25.00 lakhs, concessional
rate of interest on refinance to  tiny sector by SIDBI shall continue  and (project co st limit under NEF
Scheme has been raised to Rs.50.00 lakhs). 
19.4     Replying to the Committee’s query whether th e Indian tiny sector has attained the competitive 
resilence to face the challenges of free  imports and intense competition,  the Ministry of ARI stated that
the process of liberalization has e xposed the tiny sector to intensif ied competition  both globally and
domestically.  In order to help  building up the capabili ties of the tiny units to face the emerging
challenges, there has to be a furthe r increase in the flow of  financia l assistance to facilitate additional
capacity generation, expansion of ex isting units and improving  their capacity utiliz ation, diversification
and to enhance the competitivene ss of the sector with a th rust on technology upgradation and
modernization.

20.4  Impact of globalizat ion and liberalization on the growth and development of Agro & Rural
Industries in India.   
20.4.1  The impact of liberalization has enhanced the competitive nature of the whole industrial set up as
such. Open market mechanisms have come in place of  regulated and protected nature of pre-liberalize d 
economy. The challenge  posed by globalized econom y has enhanced and en abled nurturing of the
inherent competitive and resilient nature of the Agro and Rural Industries sector as such. 
20.4.2  The sector  mainly consists of Khadi, Village  Industries, cottage industr ies (handicrafts), Coir,
Tiny and Micro enterprises. The products of this sector  by its very nature is traditional, location specific
and exclusively indigeno us. This adds to the specialized and excl usive nature of the sector as such and
gives it a dynamic and resilient char acter. For example, herbal pro ducts, organic manure, organic food,
honey production, traditional cr afts items, etc are so exclusive by nature that it offers immense export
potential which is almost non-comp etitive in the world economy. This defines the future outlook of the
sector. The emphasis would be to highlight the exclusivity of ARI  products and its suitability to specific
local area both for production as well as marketing as it addresses the felt local needs and to develop
quality diversification and aggressively enter the world market.

20.7  CREDIT FLOW TO AGRO & RURAL INDUSTRIES 
20.7.1  Major credit flow to the Agro &Rural Industrie s is through financial inst itutions. Credit flow to
units in this sector is supported by way of Margin Money/subsidy/loan/working capital. The loan part is
accessed through the financial institutions and the subsidy and margin money part of the project is borne
form the budgetary allocations to  the concerned implementing ag ency. Problems by way of unviable
projects, cutting down financial size of the projects, lengthy procedural formalities are faced in general
by the beneficiaries or entrepreneurs in accessing credit for their units.  This may be, to a certain extent
linked to unsatisfactory r ecovery of finances advanced. Hence th e attempt is to constantly, vigorously
pursue recovery dues and at the same time ensure easy accessibility to new entrepreneurs.  
20.7.2  The Committee is of the view that continued institutional credit  flow to ARI Sector is a prio r
condition for the growth and development of Agro a nd Rural Industries, theref ore, it is suggested that
the government should take suitable steps for ch anging the mindsets of fi nancial institutions fo r
providing sufficient credit flow to all concerned im plementing agencies of Agro and Rural Industries so
that the benefits of the schemes and programme must reach to the lowest rungs of the society as is
intended at the initial stage of pol icy making . `Regional Rural Banks’ c ould be guided to play its role 
exclusively for Agro and Rural Industries. 
  
20.8  BALANCED REGIONAL   AND NATIONAL ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT. 
20.8.1  Rural industries provide the critical forum n eeded for a balanced regi onal growth due to its 
unique resilient and vibrant qualitie s as a sector which spans the Na tion as a whole. With the secto r
being a combination of traditional skills coupled with modern technology provides a very strong and
potential weapon to combat the nega tive effects of liberalization. It is an accepted fact that in ou r
country, with regional imbalances as they exist, liberalization without the presence of this sector would
have made the existing imbalances extreme and a potent threat to the objectives of rural industrialization
and poverty alleviation. It is in this scenario that this independent Ministry, focusing totally on this
sector, formulating policies to withst and the effects of libe ralization, assumes its critical role in shaping
the national economic scenario. The measures should effectively enab le the achievement of balanced
regional growth. 
20.8.2           The Committees recommends that  the Ministry of ARI s hould take concrete and
concerted and effective m easures for Agro & Rural Industries fo r striking equilibrium   for balanced
regional   growth and overall national economic growth and development.

            After examining the eligibility criteria for PMRY the Committee ha s arrived at a conclusion that

logical and rational, however, eligibility clause as regards the family income needs modification to make
it a realistic criteria.  The Com mittee feels that the family income  of Rs. 40,000  per annum hardly
fulfills the bare needs of a family  consisting of 2-3 persons.  Moreove r, the devaluation /depreciation o f

the reasons of low recovery of loans under PMRY may be construed from the fact that loan amount goes

existing limit of Rs. 40,000 to Rs. 1.5 lakh.

REPORT
 
Steel Authority of India (SAIL), the leading steel making company in India and the World’s thirteenth largest steel
producer in terms of crude steel production, is a Company registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1956 and is an
enterprise of the Government of India. SAIL was incorporated in January, 1973 as a holding company for steel and associated
input industries.  From 1973  to 1978, several steel and alloy  manufacturing companies  and iron ore mines were merged into
and  combined with SAIL’s  operation, while the Government of India (GOI) transferred the ownership  of certain consulting,
construction, mining and fire bricks operation from SAIL to other entities. 
 
  The authorized capital of SAIL is Rs. 5000 crore and the paid-up capital of the Company as on 31
st December 2002
was Rs. 4,130.40 crore of which 85.82% was held by the Government of India and the balance 14.18% by the financial
institutions/GDR-holders banks/employees/individuals etc.  The Company recorded a sales turnover of Rs. 15502 crore in
2001-02, however, due to fall in international prices of steel products,  coupled with continued sluggishness in the economy,
the price realization in the domestic market during 2001-02 declined, resulting into the post-tax net loss to the tune of Rs.
1706.89 crore during the year 2001-02.  As a result of loss, the Company has not declared a dividend for the year ended 31
st
march, 2002.  The gross margin (profit before depreciation and interest) and net loss for the nine-months ended 31 st
December, 2002 was Rs. 1334.40 crore and Rs. 545.96 crore respectively.  The company recorded a sales turnover of Rs.
13097.43 crore during this period. 
 
            Global Steel Industry for the measure part of 2001 remained a victim of slow down in demand, sliding price levels,
low realizations, losses and/or falling profits.  However, from the beginning of 2002, the industry entered a recovery phase,
with the gradual firming up of international prices and demand.  During the  financial year 2002-03, the market is signaling an
upward trend.   The year 2003 may well see a price rise in the domestic and the  international steel market.  There have been
price increases in steel products, which have been absorbed by the market.  There has been improvement in production also as
compared to last year and efforts are being made towards achieving maximum capacity utilization matching with the
increased market demand.  The company is vigorously giving greater thrust on the cost control measures during the current
year as well.  With the improvement in market demand, increase in net sales realization and cost control efforts, the company
expects much better results during the financial year 2002-03.
The turnaround in the market trends is reflected most prominently in the performance of the public sector steel giant,
Steel Authority of India Ltd. The unaudited financial results of SAIL for April-December (Q3) 2002 reveals a sharp
improvement in the performance with losses being slashed to Rs. 79 crore in Q3 ’02 - an improvement of Rs. 507 crore over
the corresponding period of the previous year. SAIL’s loss for April-December ’02 was brought to a level of Rs. 558 crore,
showing a recovery of 57 per cent over the results of the same period in 2001. This helped the company to post a cash profit
of Rs 215 crore in Q3 ’02 as against a loss of Rs 297 crore in Q3 ’01 and a cash profit of Rs. 305 crore in the first nine months
of the current financial year.  SAIL had suffered a cash loss of Rs. 434 crore during the corresponding period in the last fiscal.

IISCO & MEL.

SAIL markets and sells most of its products through in house Central Marketing Organisation (CMO) which has a
wide network  of 38 Branch Offices and 47 outlets located in major cities and towns throughout India.  International Trade
Division of SAIL looks after export of steel products to countries worldwide.  Raw materials Division manages operations of
key captive mines and quarries  of SAIL.  The captive mines of iron ore and flux meet most of the iron ore requirement and
half of the flux  requirement   of SAIL.
 
SAIL has undertaken major modernization programmes at Durgapur, Rourkela and Bokaro Steel Plants. Under the
modernization programmes, energy efficient Basic, Oxygen Furnace (BOF) technology for steel-making has been adopted in
place of obsolete Open Hearth Furnaces at Durgapur and Rourkela.  Instead of Ingot Casting, Continuous Casting facilities
have been provided in all the three Plants. The modernization projects are being funded from the internal resource of SAIL
without any budgetary support from the Government.  The total investment in modernization of the three plants is likely to be
about Rs. 12,650 crore.
 
 The main objectives of modernization are:

(ii)                Improvement in productivity and yields
(iii)               Reduction in energy consumption
(iv)              Improvement in quality of products
(v)                Reduction in cost of production
(vi)              Reduced environmental pollution

attain properly matched steady integrated operation; Improvement in quality and consistency of raw material; Upgradation of
technology; Reduction in cost of production; Pollution Control;  and Improvement in quality of steel produced

and commitments.  Subsequent to the break-up of USSR into different Nations, these manufacturing units were being
controlled by different authorities and a number of new regulations were introduced.  This resulted in delay in  manufacturing
activities.  Tyazhpromexport (TPE)’s job has suffered seriously, resulting in delays in supply of imported equipment,
structures and refractories from Russia for four global packages viz, Blast Furnace, Sinter Plant, Basic Oxygen Furnaces and

Rourkela Steel Plant was initially set up with a capacity of 1 million tonne per annum (Mtpa) of ingot steel in 1960-61
with German technical assistance. The capacity of the Plant was expanded to 1.8 Mtpa in 1969.       The main units of RSP
upto 1.8 Mtpa stage were Coke Ovens, Blast Furnaces, Steel Melting Shop, Rolling Mills consisting of Hot Rolling Mills &
Cold Rolling Mills, Electric Sheet Mill and ERW Pipe Plant. The Special Plate Mill and SW Pip~ Plant were installed later in
1976. Further, a Silicon Steel Mill, consisting of Cold Rolled Non Oriented (CRNO) and Cold Rolled Grain Oriented
(CRGO), was added in Oct'84 and Apr'89 respectively. The main saleable products of RSP are Plates, HR Coils & Sheets, CR
Coils & Sheets, Galvanised Sheets, Tin !Plates, ERW Pipes, SW Pipes and Silicon Steel Sheets.  While the 1 Mtpa stage Plant
operated, more or less, satisfactorily by reaching its rated capacity in 1964-65, the expanded capacity could never be
achieved. The best production level of 1.5 Mtpa of ingot steel was achieved in 1976-77 after which the production capacity
deteriorated. The unsatisfactory performance level was attributable to various factors like deteriorating and inconsistent
quality of raw materials and technological obsolescence. Various studies were carried out to determine the manner in  which
the optimum performance level of the Plant could be achieved. Based on these studies, a scheme for "Renovation &
Technological Upgradation"
(Modernization) of the Plant was considered.
 
The Modernisation of Rourkela Steel Plant was approved by the Government in Oct'89 at a cost of Rs.2461 crores
with FE Component of Rs.396 crores (Base date: 4th Qtr. 88). Government further 'approved in May'92 the revised cost
estimate (RCE-I) of Rs.3954 crores with FE Component of Rs.714 crores (Base date: 1 st Qtr. 92). The revised cost estimate
(RCE-II) of RSP. Modernization works out to Rs.5105.29 crore (FE: Rs.706 crore) on base date of 2nd Qtr'99.

  Modernisation Of Bokaro  Steel Plant
 
            Bokaro Steel Plant, conceived in 1959, is the fourth steel plant among the integrated steel plants in the public sector.
The Plant was conceived in 1959 as a 4 MT plant right from the conceptual stage, 1.7 MT being an intermediate stage for the
project. The construction work for the project was started in late Sixties and the Plant went into commercial production in
1972 with the commissioning of its first Blast Furnace. Steel making adopting the BOF route began a year later. The
downstream facilities -Slabbing Mill, Hot Strip Mill and Cold Rolling Mill were put into operation in stages. The. 1.7 MT
stage was completed in 1978 with the commissioning of third Blast Furnace. The work of 4 MT Expansion was. taken ~p
simultaneously and was progressively completed by Nov'90.     The entire steel making process of Bokaro Steel Plant was
based on the Ingot Casting route which was a technology prevalent in late Sixties. Considering the  various advantages of
Continuous Casting as regards to yield improvement,  conservation of energy and improved quality, Govt. of India sanctioned
Stage I  Modernisation of Bokaro Steel Plant in Jul'93 with a commissioning schedule of Jul'97. All major contracts were
awarded in 12 months. Trials for the Steel Refining Unit were started in Sep'97 and the first Continuous Casting Machine
started its trial runs in Nov'97. Subsequently, all units of Stage I Modernisation have been completed by Jan'00. With the
upgradation of the Hot Strip Mill, the quality of the finished products is of international standard and is being well accepted in
both global and domestic market. As a flat product plant, Bokaro's products include a wide range of Hot Rolled and Cold
Rolled Coils, Plates and Sheets, Galvanised Sheets and Black Plates, serving the needs of railways, tube makers and
automobile industry , L.PG cylinder manufacturers, defence and Petro-based  Industry etc. Quality conscious Bokaro is also
concerned with customers' satisfaction.
 
Approval & Implementation
 
The Modernisation (Phase-l) of Bokaro Steel Plant   was approved by the Government in Jul'93 at a cost of Rs.1625.79
crores (Base date: 1st Qtr.'93) with FE Component of Rs.283.50 crores. The revised cost (RCE-I) of Rs.1792.90 crores (Base
date: 1st Qtr.'94) with FE Component of Rs.301 crores was approved by the Government in Aug'94. The revised cost estimate
(RCE-II) of BSL Modernisation works out to Rs.2468.18 crore (FE: Rs.420.77 crore) on base date: 3rd Qtr.'98.

                  Financial & Business Restructuring in SAIL
 
A number of steps were initiated to combat the declining profitability. The Govt. of India also approved a financial and
business restructuring package  to improve the cost competitiveness of steel industry. While, the financial  restructuring
measures are aimed at mitigating the financial risk by improving the Company’s debt servicing capability, the business
restructuring measures will provide a long term competitiveness in its core business of carbon steel.
 
The financial restructuring of SAIL comprises of:
 
(i)
                  Waiver of loans advanced to it from Steel Development Fund (SDF) to a value of Rs.5073 crores and Rs.381
crores from the Govt. of India.
(ii)                Provision of Govt. Guarantee with 50% interest subsidy for loan and interest thereon of Rs.1500 crores to be
raised by SAIL from the market to finance reduction in manpower through Voluntary Retirement Scheme (VRS).
(iii)               Government guarantee for loan and interest thereon of Rs.1500 crores to be raised by SAIL from the market
primarily for meeting repayment obligation on past loans during 1999-2000.

R&D Inputs in SAIL Plants
 
The focus of R&D activities has been to improve steel technologies in SAIL with the aim to reduce cost and improve
product quality and address the market requirements of new value added products.
 
The R&D Centre of SAIL (RDCIS) has contributed significantly in the development of a number of Process
Technologies.  Some of these are:
 
(i)
                  Continuous casting of CRNO steel at RSP.  This has helped RSP to close down ingot casting shop and high
energy consuming slabbing mill.  As a result, RSP became the first plant in SAIL to route 100% of production through
continuous casting.
 
(ii)
                Introduction of innovative technologies, use of higher percentage of imported coal and optimization of process
parameters have significantly improved blast furnace productivity in SAIL plants.

 Marketing policy of SAIL for improving market share
 
The prime quality Iron & Mild Steel materials produced by SAIL Plants (excluding IISCO) are sold through Central
Marketing Organisation (CMO).
 
            With a view to evolve a sales plan attuned to the market conditions, a detailed exercise is undertaken before the
commencement of each financial year which inter alia include plantwise, productwise, segmentwise sales plan keeping in
view the demand and supply scenario in the country as well as production capability of each of the plants of SAIL.
 
            Simultaneously the order booking schemes and strategies are finalized.
 
            In order to compete in the highly competitive market, marketing strategies are reoriented based on the prevailing
market conditions and requirements and customers’ expectations.  Some of the marketing strategies presently adopted by
SAIL are as under :-
 
(i)
                  Orienting product-mix to suit market requirements.
(ii)                Adoption of Key Account Management Process to provide total service to major / strategic accounts.
(iii)               Special emphasis on marketing value added products.
(iv)              Development and nurturing long term relationships with customers by entering into MOU/ Annual tie ups with
them
(v)                Increasing sales through net work of dealers.
(vi)              Offering full package of steel materials to projects.
(vii)             Increasing  availability of finished steel through conversion.

Help required from the Government
(A)       Coal
i)
                    Steep price increase by CIL over the years has been putting lot of pressure on our competitiveness in the market.
Long-term pricing mechanism is being discussed between SAIL and coal companies, however, it is proposed that
there should be an independent arbitrator to look into the pricing mechanism of domestic coking coal.
ii)                   The availability of indigenous coal is depleting at a very fast rate, thus forcing higher usage of imported coking
coal in the coal blend and consequent pressure on ports. Haldia port is most economical for transportation of
imported coal as three integrated steel plants of SAIL are located in the Eastern Region. Capacity at Haldia  port is
inadequate for handling coal for supply to these steel plants. Moreover, due to low draft at Haldia Port, SAIL is
constrained to part unload the ships at Vizag or Paradip port before bringing it to Haldia port. Help is required for
upgradation of Haldia port.
 
(B)   Power
 
Production in steel plants has been affected in H-1 by inconsistencies in power supply.  This was especially so
in eastern region where four of SAIL’s plants are located.  There were a large number of total power failures,
voltage dips and frequency of power supply remained abnormally high for long durations.
 
High frequency of power supply resulted in loss of captive power generation, equipment damage and erosion
in life of rotating equipment, apart from increased power bill due to higher drawal of power.
 
It is expected that incidence of high frequency will come down after the proposed interconnections of Eastern
grid with North/South in October/ November 2002. However, it is felt that appreciable improvement can be
obtained only by implementation of ‘Availability Based Tariff’.
 
 
(C)             To meet the full compliance of Pollution Control norms in Coke Ovens as per the directives of MOEF, large
scale financial investment is called for.  A provision of Rs. 1000 crores has been made in 10
th Five Year Plan
which will allow us to take up rebuilding of not more than 6 batteries over the next 5 years.  If SAIL has to stick to
the stringent regulatory requirement to make all 21 batteries fully compliant within a tightened time frame, SAIL
will have to seek financial assistance from Government to ensure full compliance in batteries.  Towards this end,
SAIL has proposed Rs. 80 crore assistance from Govt. in 2003-04 BE.
